sentence: This paper investigates why recent generative AI models outperform humans in data visualization knowledge tasks.
Systematic comparative analysis of responses to visualization questions was conducted.
Differences exist between two ChatGPT models and human outputs over rhetorical structure, knowledge breadth, and perceptual quality.
ChatGPT-4, as a more advanced model, displays a hybrid of characteristics from both humans and ChatGPT-3.5.
The two models were generally favored over human responses.
Strengths in coverage and breadth, and emphasis on technical and task-oriented visualization feedback collectively shaped higher overall quality.
Implications are drawn for advancing user experiences based on the potential of LLMs and human perception over their capabilities.
The findings are relevant to broader applications of AI.
The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative visual analytics systems has transformed data-driven insights.
Significant challenges persist in accurately interpreting users' analytical and interaction intents.
Language inputs offer flexibility but often lack precision, making the expression of complex intents inefficient, error-prone, and time-intensive.
We investigate the design space of multimodal interactions for generative visual analytics through a literature review and pilot brainstorming sessions.
We introduce a highly extensible workflow that integrates multiple LLM agents for intent inference and visualization generation.
We develop InterChat, a generative visual analytics system that combines direct manipulation of visual elements with natural language inputs.
This integration enables precise intent communication and supports progressive, visually driven exploratory data analyses.
InterChat employs effective prompt engineering, contextual interaction linking, and intuitive visualization and interaction designs.
InterChat bridges the gap between user interactions and LLM-driven visualizations, enhancing both interpretability and usability.
Extensive evaluations, including two usage scenarios, a user study, and expert feedback, demonstrate the effectiveness of InterChat.
Results show significant improvements in the accuracy and efficiency of handling complex visual analytics tasks.
The findings highlight the potential of multimodal interactions to redefine user engagement and analytical depth in generative visual analytics.
Translating natural language to visualization (NL2VIS) has shown great promise for visual data analysis.
NL2VIS remains a challenging task that requires multiple low-level implementations, such as natural language processing and visualization design.
Recent advancements in pre-trained large language models (LLMs) are opening new avenues for generating visualizations from natural language.
The lack of a comprehensive and reliable benchmark hinders our understanding of LLMs' capabilities in visualization generation.
We propose a new NL2VIS benchmark called VisEval.
VisEval includes a high-quality and large-scale dataset.
The dataset includes 2,524 representative queries covering 146 databases, paired with accurately labeled ground truths.
We advocate for a comprehensive automated evaluation methodology covering multiple dimensions, including validity, legality, and readability.
VisEval systematically scans for potential issues with a number of heterogeneous checkers.
VisEval provides reliable and trustworthy evaluation outcomes.
We run VisEval on a series of state-of-the-art LLMs.
Our evaluation reveals prevalent challenges in visualization generation.
Our evaluation delivers essential insights for future advancements in NL2VIS.
Deep research has revolutionized data analysis.
Data scientists still devote substantial time to manually crafting visualizations.
There is a need for robust automation from natural language queries.
Current systems struggle with complex datasets containing multiple files and iterative refinement.
Existing approaches, including simple single- or multi-agent systems, often oversimplify the task.
Existing approaches focus on initial query parsing while failing to robustly manage data complexity, code errors, or final visualization quality.
This paper reframes the challenge of visualization automation as a collaborative multi-agent problem.
We introduce CoDA, a multi-agent system that employs specialized LLM agents for metadata analysis, task planning, code generation, and self-reflection.
We formalize the CoDA pipeline, demonstrating how metadata-focused analysis bypasses token limits.
Quality-driven refinement in CoDA ensures robustness.
Extensive evaluations show CoDA achieves substantial gains in the overall score.
CoDA outperforms competitive baselines by up to 41.5%.
This work demonstrates that the future of visualization automation lies in integrated, collaborative agentic workflows.
This paper evaluates the visualization literacy of modern Large Language Models (LLMs).
A novel prompting technique called Charts-of-Thought is introduced.
Three state-of-the-art LLMs (Claude-3.7-sonnet, GPT-4.5-preview, and Gemini-2.0-pro) were tested on the Visualization Literacy Assessment Test (VLAT).
The tests used standard prompts and the structured Charts-of-Thought approach.
The Charts-of-Thought method guides LLMs through a systematic data extraction, verification, and analysis process before answering visualization questions.
Claude-3.7-sonnet achieved a score of 50.17 using the Charts-of-Thought method, far exceeding the human baseline of 28.82.
The Charts-of-Thought approach improved performance across all models, with score increases of 21.8% for GPT-4.5, 9.4% for Gemini-2.0, and 13.5% for Claude-3.7 compared to standard prompting.
The performance gains were consistent across original and modified VLAT charts.
Claude correctly answered 100% of questions for several chart types that previously challenged LLMs.
Modern multimodal LLMs can surpass human performance on visualization literacy tasks when given the proper analytical framework.
These findings establish a new benchmark for LLM visualization literacy.
Structured prompting strategies are important for complex visual interpretation tasks.
Charts-of-Thought could enhance the accessibility of visualizations, potentially benefiting individuals with visual impairments or lower visualization literacy.

Systems that support users in the automatic creation of visualizations must address several subtasks, including understanding the semantics of data, enumerating relevant visualization goals, and generating visualization specifications.
Visualization generation is posed as a multi-stage generation problem in this work.
Well-orchestrated pipelines based on large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT/GPT-4 and image generation models (IGMs) are argued to be suitable for addressing visualization generation tasks.
LIDA is a novel tool for generating grammar-agnostic visualizations and infographics.
LIDA comprises four modules: a SUMMARIZER, a GOAL EXPLORER, a VISGENERATOR, and an INFOGRAPHER.
The SUMMARIZER module converts data into a rich but compact natural language summary.
The GOAL EXPLORER module enumerates visualization goals given the data.
The VISGENERATOR module generates, refines, executes, and filters visualization code.
The INFOGRAPHER module yields data-faithful stylized graphics using IGMs.
LIDA provides a Python API and a hybrid user interface for interactive chart, infographic, and data story generation.
Vision Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate promising chart comprehension capabilities.
Prior explorations of VLMs' visualization literacy have been limited to assessing their response correctness.
Prior explorations of VLMs' visualization literacy fail to explore their internal reasoning.
Attention-guided class activation maps (AG-CAM) were adapted for VLMs to visualize the influence and importance of input features (image and text) on model responses.
Using AG-CAM, an examination of four open-source (ChartGemma, Janus 1B and 7B, and LLaVA) and two closed-source (GPT-4o, Gemini) models was conducted.
The examination compared the performance of the models and, for the open-source models, their AG-CAM results.
ChartGemma, a 3B parameter VLM fine-tuned for chart question-answering (QA), outperformed other open-source models.
ChartGemma exhibited performance on par with significantly larger closed-source VLMs.
VLMs exhibit spatial reasoning by accurately localizing key chart features.
VLMs exhibit semantic reasoning by associating visual elements with corresponding data values and query tokens.
This approach is the first to demonstrate the use of AG-CAM on early fusion VLM architectures, which are widely used, and for chart QA.
Preliminary evidence shows that AG-CAM results can align with human reasoning.
Promising open-source VLM results pave the way for transparent and reproducible research in AI visualization literacy.
Code and Supplemental Materials: https://osf.io/fp3rg.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown great potential in intelligent visualization systems, especially for domain-specific applications.
Integrating LLMs into visualization systems presents challenges.
We categorize these challenges into three alignments: domain problems with LLMs, visualization with LLMs, and interaction with LLMs.
To achieve these alignments, we propose a framework to guide the application of fine-tuned LLMs to enhance visual interactions for domain-specific tasks.
We outline a workflow to guide the application of fine-tuned LLMs to enhance visual interactions for domain-specific tasks.
These alignment challenges are critical in education because of the need for an intelligent visualization system to support beginners' self-regulated learning.
We apply the framework to education and introduce Tailor-Mind, an interactive visualization system designed to facilitate self-regulated learning for artificial intelligence beginners.
Drawing on insights from a preliminary study, we identify self-regulated learning tasks to guide visualization design and tuning data construction.
Drawing on insights from a preliminary study, we identify fine-tuning objectives to guide visualization design and tuning data construction.
Our focus on aligning visualization with fine-tuned LLM makes Tailor-Mind more like a personalized tutor.
Tailor-Mind supports interactive recommendations to help beginners better achieve their learning goals.
Model performance evaluations and user studies confirm that Tailor-Mind improves the self-regulated learning experience.
Model performance evaluations and user studies effectively validate the proposed framework.
We investigate the potential of leveraging the code-generating capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to support exploratory visual analysis (EVA) via conversational user interfaces (CUIs).
We developed a technology probe that was deployed through two studies with a total of 50 data workers to explore the structure and flow of visual analytic conversations during EVA.
We analyzed conversations from both studies using thematic analysis.

We derived a state transition diagram summarizing the conversational flow between four states of participant utterances (Analytic Tasks, Editing Operations, Elaborations and Enrichments, and Directive Commands) and two states of Generative AI (GenAI) agent responses (visualization, text).
We describe the capabilities and limitations of GenAI agents according to each state and transitions between states as three co-occurring loops: analysis elaboration, refinement, and explanation.
We discuss our findings as future research trajectories to improve the experiences of data workers using GenAI.
The code and data are available at https://osf.io/6wxpa.
Natural-language-to-visualization (NL2VIS) systems based on large language models (LLMs) have substantially improved the accessibility of data visualization.
The adoption of NL2VIS systems is hindered by the absence of standardized evaluation metrics.
The adoption of NL2VIS systems is hindered by the inherent underspecification of natural language descriptions, which allows multiple valid visualizations for the same query.
VegaChat is a framework for generating, validating, and assessing declarative visualizations from natural language.
VegaChat introduces Spec Score, a deterministic metric that measures specification-level similarity without invoking an LLM.
VegaChat introduces Vision Score, a library-agnostic, image-based metric that leverages a multimodal LLM to assess chart similarity and prompt compliance.
VegaChat is evaluated on the NLV Corpus and on the annotated subset of ChartLLM.
VegaChat achieves near-zero rates of invalid or empty visualizations.
Spec Score and Vision Score exhibit strong correlation with human judgments, with Pearson correlations of 0.65 and 0.71, respectively.
The proposed metrics support consistent, cross-library comparison.
The code and evaluation artifacts for VegaChat are available at https://zenodo.org/records/17062309.
Formal representations of the visualization design space consolidate design practices into a shared resource.
Formal representations of the visualization design space enable automated reasoning and interpretable design recommendations.
Prior approaches typically depend on fixed, manually authored rules.
Fixed, manually authored rules make it difficult to build novel representations or extend them for different visualization domains.
We propose data-driven methods that automatically synthesize visualization design knowledge bases.
Our methods extract candidate design features from a visualization corpus.
Our methods select features forward and backward.
Our methods render the final knowledge base.
In our benchmark evaluation compared to Draco 2, our synthesized knowledge base offers general and interpretable design features.
In our benchmark evaluation compared to Draco 2, our synthesized knowledge base improves the accuracy of predicting effective designs by 1-15% in varied training and test sets.
When applied to genomics visualization, the synthesized knowledge base includes sensible features with accuracy up to 97%.
The results demonstrate the applicability of our approach to other visualization domains.
Data visualization creators often lack formal training, resulting in a knowledge gap in design practice.
Large-language models such as ChatGPT, with their vast internet-scale training data, offer transformative potential to address this gap.
In this study, we used both qualitative and quantitative methods to investigate how well ChatGPT can address visualization design questions.
We quantitatively compared the ChatGPT-generated responses with anonymous online Human replies to data visualization questions on the VisGuides user forum.
We conducted a qualitative user study examining the reactions and attitudes of practitioners toward ChatGPT as a visualization design assistant.
Participants were asked to bring their visualizations and design questions and received feedback from both Human experts and ChatGPT in randomized order.
Our findings from both studies underscore ChatGPT’s strengths—particularly its ability to rapidly generate diverse design options.
Our findings highlight areas for improvement, such as nuanced contextual understanding and fluid interaction dynamics beyond the chat interface.
We discuss design considerations for future LLM-based design feedback systems.
Empirical research on perception and cognition has laid the foundation for visualization design.
Empirical research is often distilled into practical guidelines intended to support effective chart creation.
It remains unclear how well research-driven insights are reflected in the guidelines practitioners actually use.
This paper investigates the research-practice gap in visualization design guidelines through a mixed-methods approach.
Design guidelines were collected from practitioner-facing sources and empirical studies from academic venues to assess their alignment.
Surveys and interviews were conducted with practitioners and researchers to examine their experiences, perceptions, and challenges surrounding the development and use of design guidelines.
Findings reveal misalignment between empirical evidence and widely used guidelines.
Findings reveal differing perspectives between communities.
Findings reveal key barriers that contribute to the persistence of the research-practice gap.
We introduce VL2NL, a Large Language Model (LLM) framework that generates rich and diverse NL datasets using only Vega-Lite specifications as input.
VL2NL streamlines the development of Natural Language Interfaces (NLIs) for data visualization.
To synthesize relevant chart semantics accurately and enhance syntactic diversity in each NL dataset, VL2NL leverages a guided discovery incorporated into prompting.
Guided discovery allows LLMs to steer themselves to create faithful NL datasets in a self-directed manner.
VL2NL uses a score-based paraphrasing to augment NL syntax along four language axes.
We present a new collection of 1,981 real-world Vega-Lite specifications.
The new Vega-Lite collection has increased diversity and complexity compared to existing chart collections.
When tested on our chart collection, VL2NL extracted chart semantics with 89.4% accuracy for L1 captions.
When tested on our chart collection, VL2NL extracted chart semantics with 76.0% accuracy for L2 captions.
VL2NL demonstrated generating and paraphrasing utterances and questions with greater diversity compared to the benchmarks.
Our NL datasets and framework can be utilized in real-world scenarios.
The codes and chart collection are available at https://github.com/hyungkwonko/chart-llm.
Incorporating natural language input has the potential to improve the capabilities of biomedical data discovery interfaces.
User interface elements and visualizations are still powerful tools for interacting with data.
In the prototype system YAC (Yet Another Chatbot), natural language and interactive visualizations are integrated.
YAC uses a tool-calling multi-agent system to generate declarative output.
The declarative output is interpreted to render linked interactive visualizations and apply data filters.
Adjustment widgets are included to allow users to directly modify the structured output.
Structured text is generated to clarify user intent, notify users of system boundaries, and explain aspects of the data with live data element links.
A user study was conducted with domain experts to surface areas where YAC can be improved.
The capabilities and design of the system are analyzed with an evaluation of its technical dimensions.
Biomedical research data portals are essential resources for scientific inquiry.
Interactive exploratory visualizations are an integral component for querying data repositories.
Machine learning is increasingly being integrated into visualization systems to create natural language interfaces.
Natural language interfaces allow questions about data to be answered with visualizations and enable follow-up questions to build on the previous state.
This paper introduces a framework that takes abstract low-level questions about data and a visualization grammar specification that can answer such a question.
The framework reifies abstract questions with data entities and fields that meet certain constraints.
The framework paraphrases the question language to produce the final collection of realized data-question-visualization triplets.
The framework links foundational elements together to construct chains of queries, visualizations, and follow-up queries.
We developed an open-source review interface for evaluating the results of these datasets.
We applied this framework to five biomedical research data repositories.
The application of the framework resulted in DQVis, a dataset of 1.08 million data-question-visualization triplets and 11.4 thousand two-step question samples.
Five visualization experts provided feedback on the generated dataset through our review interface.
We present a summary of the experts' input and publish the full reviews as an additional resource alongside the dataset.
The DQVis dataset and generation code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HIDIVE/DQVis and https://github.com/hms-dbmi/DQVis-Generation.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed numerous technological domains within the database community.
This paper examines the application of LLMs in text-to-visualization (text-to-vis).
The advancement of natural language processing technologies has made natural language interfaces more accessible and intuitive for visualizing tabular data.
Current methods such as Seq2Vis, ncNet, and RGVisNet for transforming natural language queries into DV commands underperform despite utilizing advanced neural network architectures.
There is significant room for improvement in current text-to-vis methods.
This paper introduces Prompt4Vis, a novel framework that leverages LLMs and In-context learning to enhance the generation of data visualizations from natural language.
In-context learning’s effectiveness is highly dependent on the selection of examples, making it critical to optimize this aspect.
Encoding the full database schema of a query is costly and can lead to inaccuracies.
The Prompt4Vis framework includes an example mining module that identifies highly effective examples to enhance In-context learning capabilities for text-to-vis applications.
The Prompt4Vis framework includes a schema filtering module designed to streamline database schemas.

Comprehensive testing on the NVBench dataset shows that Prompt4Vis significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art model, RGVisNet, by approximately 35.9% on development sets and 71.3% on test sets.
Prompt4Vis is the first framework to incorporate In-context learning for enhancing text-to-vis.
Prompt4Vis marks a pioneering step in the text-to-vis domain.
Real-world visualization tasks involve complex, multi-modal requirements that extend beyond simple text-to-chart generation.
Real-world visualization tasks require reference images, code examples, and iterative refinement.
Current systems exhibit fundamental limitations such as single-modality input, one-shot generation, and rigid workflows.
LLM-based approaches show potential for addressing complex requirements in visualization tasks.
LLM-based approaches introduce reliability challenges including catastrophic failures and infinite loop susceptibility.
We propose MultiVis-Agent, a logic rule-enhanced multi-agent framework for reliable multi-modal and multi-scenario visualization generation.
Our approach introduces a four-layer logic rule framework that provides mathematical guarantees for system reliability while maintaining flexibility.
Unlike traditional rule-based systems, our logic rules are mathematical constraints that guide LLM reasoning rather than replacing it.
We formalize the MultiVis task spanning four scenarios from basic generation to iterative refinement.
We develop MultiVis-Bench, a benchmark with over 1,000 cases for multi-modal visualization evaluation.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves a 75.63% visualization score on challenging tasks.
Our approach significantly outperforms baselines, which achieve scores between 57.54% and 62.79%.
Our approach achieves task completion rates of 99.58% and code execution success rates of 94.56%.
Without logic rules, task completion rates and code execution success rates are 74.48% and 65.10%, respectively.
Our approach successfully addresses both complexity and reliability challenges in automated visualization generation.
A wide range of visualization authoring interfaces enable the creation of highly customized visualizations.
Prioritizing expressiveness often impedes the learnability of the authoring interface.
The diversity of users, such as varying computational skills and prior experiences in user interfaces, makes it challenging for a single authoring interface to satisfy the needs of a broad audience.
In this paper, we introduce a framework to balance learnability and expressivity in a visualization authoring system.

Adopting insights from learnability studies, such as multimodal interaction and visualization literacy, we explore the design space of blending multiple visualization authoring interfaces for supporting authoring tasks in a complementary and flexible manner.

To evaluate the effectiveness of blending interfaces, we implemented a proof-of-concept system, Blace, that combines four common visualization authoring interfaces—template-based, shelf configuration, natural language, and code editor—that are tightly linked to one another.
Blace helps users easily relate unfamiliar interfaces to more familiar ones.
Using the system, we conducted a user study with 12 domain experts who regularly visualize genomics data as part of their analysis workflow.
Participants with varied visualization and programming backgrounds were able to successfully reproduce unfamiliar visualization examples without a guided tutorial in the study.
Feedback from a post-study qualitative questionnaire suggests that blending interfaces enabled participants to learn the system easily.
Blending interfaces assisted participants in confidently editing unfamiliar visualization grammar in the code editor, enabling expressive customization.
Reflecting on our study results and the design of our system, we discuss the different interaction patterns that we identified and design implications for blending visualization authoring interfaces.
The field of data visualisation has long aimed to devise solutions for generating visualisations directly from natural language text.
Research in Natural Language Interfaces (NLIs) has contributed towards the development of techniques for generating visualisations from natural language text.
The implementation of workable NLIs has always been challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of natural language.
Unclear and poorly written user queries pose problems for existing language models in discerning user intent.

This study uniquely proposes leveraging the advancements in pre-trained large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and GPT-3 to convert free-form natural language directly into code for appropriate visualisations.
This paper presents a novel system, Chat2VIS, which takes advantage of the capabilities of LLMs.
Chat2VIS demonstrates how, with effective prompt engineering, the complex problem of language understanding can be solved more efficiently.
Chat2VIS results in simpler and more accurate end-to-end solutions than prior approaches.

Chat2VIS shows that LLMs together with the proposed prompts offer a reliable approach to rendering visualisations from natural language queries, even when queries are highly misspecified and underspecified.
This solution presents a significant reduction in costs for the development of NLI systems.
This solution attains greater visualisation inference abilities compared to traditional NLP approaches that use hand-crafted grammar rules and tailored models.
This study presents how LLM prompts can be constructed in a way that preserves data security and privacy.
This study presents how LLM prompts can be constructed in a way that is generalisable to different datasets.
This work compares the performance of GPT-3, Codex, and ChatGPT across several case studies.
This work contrasts the performances of GPT-3, Codex, and ChatGPT with prior studies.
There exists a gap between visualization design guidelines and their application in visualization tools.
Empirical studies can provide design guidance.

We lack a formal framework for representing design knowledge, integrating results across studies, and applying this knowledge in automated design tools that promote effective encodings and facilitate visual exploration.
We propose modeling visualization design knowledge as a collection of constraints.
We propose a method to learn weights for soft constraints from experimental data.
Using constraints, we can take theoretical design knowledge and express it in a concrete, extensible, and testable form.
The resulting models can recommend visualization designs.
The resulting models can easily be augmented with additional constraints or updated weights.
We implement our approach in Draco, a constraint-based system based on Answer Set Programming (ASP).
We demonstrate how to construct increasingly sophisticated automated visualization design systems.
These systems include those based on weights learned directly from the results of graphical perception experiments.
Natural Language to Visualization (NL2Vis) seeks to convert natural-language descriptions into visual representations of given tables.
NL2Vis empowers users to derive insights from large-scale data.
Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in automating code generation to transform tabular data into accessible visualizations.
LLMs often struggle with complex queries that require reasoning across multiple tables.
We propose a collaborative agent workflow, termed nvAgent, for NL2Vis.

nvAgent comprises three agents: a processor agent for database processing and context filtering, a composer agent for planning visualization generation, and a validator agent for code translation and output verification.
Comprehensive evaluations on the new VisEval benchmark demonstrate that nvAgent consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines.
nvAgent achieves a 7.88% improvement in single-table scenarios.
nvAgent achieves a 9.23% improvement in multi-table scenarios.
Qualitative analyses highlight that nvAgent maintains nearly a 20% performance margin over previous models.
nvAgent underscores its capacity to produce high-quality visual representations from complex, heterogeneous data sources.
Recent chart-authoring systems increasingly focus on natural-language input.
Natural-language input enables users to form a mental image of the chart they wish to create and express this intent using spoken instructions.
These systems are predominantly trained on typed instructions written while viewing the target chart.
The cognitive processes for describing an existing chart differ from those for creating a new chart.
The structural differences in the corresponding prompts remain underexplored.
We present empirical findings on the structural differences among spoken imagined-chart instructions, typed imagined-chart instructions, and typed existing-chart instructions for chart creation.
Imagined-chart prompts contain richer command formats, element specifications, and complex linguistic features, especially in spoken instructions.
We compare the performance of systems trained on spoken imagined-chart data versus typed existing-chart data.
The system trained on spoken imagined-chart data outperforms the system trained on typed existing-chart data on both voice and text input.
This highlights the necessity of targeted training on spoken imagined-chart data.
We conclude with design guidelines for chart-authoring systems to improve performance in real-world scenarios.
Design studies aim to develop visualization solutions for real-world problems across various application domains.
The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has introduced new opportunities to enhance the design study process.
LLMs provide capabilities such as creative problem-solving, data handling, and insightful analysis.
There remains a lack of systematic understanding of how LLMs can effectively assist researchers in visualization-specific design studies.
We conducted a multi-stage qualitative study to fill this gap.
The study involved 30 design study researchers from diverse backgrounds and expertise levels.
We used in-depth interviews and carefully-designed questionnaires to investigate strategies for utilizing LLMs.
We investigated the challenges encountered and the practices used to overcome them.
We compiled the roles that LLMs can play across different stages of the design study process.
Our findings highlight practical implications to inform visualization practitioners.
Our findings provide a framework for leveraging LLMs to facilitate the design study process in visualization research.
Natural language interfaces (NLIs) for data visualization are becoming increasingly popular both in academic research and in commercial software.
There is a lack of empirical understanding of how people specify visualizations through natural language.
An online study was conducted with 102 participants to bridge this gap.
Participants were shown a series of ten visualizations for a given dataset.
Participants were asked to provide utterances they would pose to generate the displayed charts.
The curated list of utterances generated from the study is provided below.
This corpus of utterances can be used to evaluate existing NLIs for data visualization.
This corpus can also be used for creating new systems and models to generate visualizations from natural language utterances.
The use of natural language interfaces (NLIs) to create charts is becoming increasingly popular due to the intuitiveness of natural language interactions.
A key challenge in using NLIs for chart creation is accurately capturing user intents and transforming them into proper chart specifications.
Users' natural language inputs are generally abstract, being ambiguous or under-specified, without a clear specification of visual encodings.
Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have exhibited superior performance in understanding and generating natural language, demonstrating great potential for downstream tasks.
We propose ChartGPT, a system for generating charts from abstract natural language inputs.
LLMs struggle to address complex logic problems.
To enable the model to accurately specify complex parameters and perform operations in chart generation, we decompose the generation process into a step-by-step reasoning pipeline.
The step-by-step reasoning pipeline ensures the model only needs to reason a single and specific sub-task during each run.
LLMs are pre-trained on general datasets, which might be biased for the task of chart generation.
We create a dataset consisting of abstract utterances and charts to provide adequate visualization knowledge.
We improve model performance through fine-tuning on the created dataset.
We design an interactive interface for ChartGPT that allows users to check and modify the intermediate outputs of each step.
The effectiveness of the proposed system is evaluated through quantitative evaluations and a user study.
Genomics experts rely on visualization to extract and share insights from complex and large-scale datasets.
There is an increasing need for platforms that aid experts in authoring customized visualizations for both exploration and communication of insights.
A variety of interactive techniques have been proposed for authoring data visualizations, such as template editing, shelf configuration, natural language input, and code editors.
It remains unclear how genomics experts create visualizations and which techniques best support their visualization tasks and needs.
Two user studies were conducted with genomics researchers.
The first study involved semi-structured interviews (n=20) to identify the tasks, user contexts, and current visualization authoring techniques.
The second study was an exploratory study (n=13) using visual probes to elicit users’ intents and desired techniques when creating visualizations.

Our contributions include a characterization of how visualization authoring is currently utilized in genomics visualization, identifying limitations and benefits in light of common criteria for authoring tools.
Our contributions include generalizable design implications for genomics visualization authoring tools based on our findings on task- and user-specific usefulness of authoring techniques.
All supplemental materials are available at https://osf.io/bdj4v/.
Generative models have received a lot of attention in many areas of academia and the industry.
Generative models are capable of tasks such as the invention of images given a prompt and the generation of concrete code to solve programming issues.
These tasks fall within two distinct categories of requirements, ranging from 'creativity' to 'precision', as characterized by Bing Chat, which employs ChatGPT-4 as its backbone.
Visualization practitioners and researchers have wondered to what extent generative models could accomplish their work more efficiently.
Several works in the literature have utilized generative models for the creation of visualizations.
Some tools, such as Lida, incorporate generative models as part of their pipeline.
To the authors' knowledge, no systematic approach for testing the capabilities of generative models has been published, which includes both extensive and in-depth evaluation.

The goal of this study is to fill the gap with a systematic approach that analyzes three elements: whether Large Language Models are capable of correctly generating a large variety of charts, what libraries they can deal with effectively, and how far we can go to configure individual charts.
To achieve this objective, a diverse set of charts commonly utilized in data visualization was initially selected.
A set of generic prompts was developed to generate the selected charts.
The performance of different Large Language Models and libraries was analyzed.
The results include the set of prompts and the data sources.
The results also include an analysis of the performance with different configurations.
Data visualization is a fundamental tool in genomics research, enabling the exploration, interpretation, and communication of complex genomic features.
Machine learning models show promise for transforming data into insightful visualizations.
Current machine learning models lack the training foundation for domain-specific tasks in genomics.
We present a framework for generating a dataset that pairs abstract, low-level questions about genomics data with corresponding visualizations.
Our approach builds on prior work with statistical plots and adapts to the complexity of genomics data and the specialized representations used to depict them.
We incorporate multiple linked queries and visualizations, along with justifications for design choices, figure captions, and image alt-texts for each item in the dataset.
We use genomics data retrieved from three distinct genomics data repositories (4DN, ENCODE, Chromoscope) to produce GQVis.
The GQVis dataset consists of 1.14 million single-query data points, 628k query pairs, and 589k query chains.
The GQVis dataset and generation code are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HIDIVE/GQVis and https://github.com/hms-dbmi/GQVis-Generation.
Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on vast corpora.
LLMs have the potential to encode visualization design knowledge and best practices.
If LLMs fail to encode visualization design knowledge, they might provide unreliable visualization recommendations.
The study investigates what visualization design preferences LLMs have learned.
We contribute DracoGPT, a method for extracting, modeling, and assessing visualization design preferences from LLMs.
To assess varied tasks, we develop two pipelines—DracoGPT-Rank and DracoGPT-Recommend.
DracoGPT-Rank models LLMs prompted to rank visual encoding specifications.
DracoGPT-Recommend models LLMs prompted to recommend visual encoding specifications.
We use Draco as a shared knowledge base to represent LLM design preferences.
We compare LLM design preferences to best practices from empirical research.
DracoGPT can accurately model the preferences expressed by LLMs.
DracoGPT enables analysis of LLM preferences in terms of Draco design constraints.
Across a suite of backing LLMs, DracoGPT-Rank and DracoGPT-Recommend moderately agree with each other.
DracoGPT-Rank and DracoGPT-Recommend substantially diverge from guidelines drawn from human subjects experiments.
Future work can expand Draco's knowledge base to model a richer set of preferences.
Future work can provide a robust and cost-effective stand-in for LLMs.
Draco introduced a constraint-based framework to model visualization design in an extensible and testable form.
Draco provides a way to abstract design guidelines from theoretical and empirical studies.

Genomic visualization specifications vary considerably in authoring complexity, from single-track charts to interactive genome browsers.

The main point of failure was consistent across schemes: no scheme rendered the cytoband track correctly.
Agentic schemes came closer to a recognizable cytoband than the baselines.
Agentic schemes most consistently generated the brush mark for overview-to-detail linking.

This regression suggests that when the model must simultaneously reason about an analytical question and compose a multiview visualization, interaction features are among the first things to be dropped.
This is consistent with our earlier finding on the interaction and coordination dimension (D4), where linking emerged as a weak area.
The iterative nature of the agentic schemes is visible in the step-by-step evolution of individual runs.
In the Multi Agents + Reviewer scheme, the QDA agent first corrected a data transformation that had been misapplied in earlier iterations.
The Reviewer subsequently added a cytoband track for navigational context.
This incremental layering of fixes and additions illustrates how the separation of concerns across agents can lead to cumulative improvements.
Non-agentic baselines did not produce cumulative improvements.
A run from the Single Agent + Reviewer scheme shows another interesting progression.
The generalist author initially produced gene annotations with typical failures also seen in Direct Generation: no directionality, missing labels, overplotted text.
Over successive iterations, the author refined the gene track to correctly show strand direction and readable labels.
The author changed an overlaid line encoding to a stratified arrangement to improve comparison effectiveness.
A capable generalist agent can self-correct on canonical genomic encodings through iterative refinement alone.
Agentic schemes were the strongest predictor of perceived quality in our evaluation.

The advantage of agentic schemes was consistent across complexity levels.

The Fixed Pipeline is a hand-crafted three-step decomposition with dedicated prompts and domain-specific guidelines.
The Fixed Pipeline performed worse than a single unconstrained LLM call given only the grammar documentation.
A structured pipeline is arguably the most natural next step after Direct Generation.
Direct Generation is the approach a practitioner would try first when one-shot results fall short.
Substantial effort was invested in the design of the Fixed Pipeline, iterating on prompt engineering for data resolution, encoding selection, and view composition.
Many small failures persisted in the Fixed Pipeline, including incorrect field mappings, misapplied genomics conventions, and broken interactions between views.
Issues in the Fixed Pipeline were especially pronounced for specifications involving brushing, overview-detail coordination, or semantic zoom.
A single change in specifications like brushing, overview-detail coordination, or semantic zoom can cascade across views and encodings.
Further prompt engineering did not resolve the error accumulation in the Fixed Pipeline.
Using multiple specialist agents did not meaningfully improve output quality.
Adding a reviewer did not meaningfully improve output quality.
A single agent achieved the same perceived quality as more complex configurations.
A single agent achieved the lowest cost.
Our per-step analysis offers some insight into why.
All agents could edit the specification.
Three agents that handle primary authoring (QDA, VEC, and Single) contributed comparable per-step improvements.
Agents operating at a higher level of abstraction contributed less to per-step improvements.
L&S, responsible for layout and coordination, showed smaller per-step improvements.
The reviewer showed the least contribution of all agents.

The findings suggest that simply adding more agents to a complex visualization authoring task is not inherently beneficial.
The benefit of agentic authoring lies in how tightly the agent’s feedback mechanism is coupled to the grammar.
Currently, agents rely on rendered screenshots, which provide holistic but coarse feedback.
Finer-grained tools, such as per-track validation, sub-view rendering, or interaction-level debugging, could let agents inspect and correct more precisely.
For grammars where syntactic correctness does not guarantee semantic validity, finer-grained tools are particularly important.
Tools would likely deliver larger gains than adding agents.

Future designs might scaffold the reviewer role to act on the issues it identifies rather than defaulting to passive critique.
Evaluation of LLM-based visualization authoring has largely relied on automated benchmarks.

In this work, we introduced a user proxy agent that simulates realistic clarification dialogues across three levels of query ambiguity.
The user proxy agent allows a single dataset of specifications to approximate how real users with varying levels of specificity might interact with the system.
The expected moderation by query ambiguity did not materialize in our results.
It remains open whether agentic schemes handle ambiguity well through their iterative process.
It remains open whether the proxy, which had access to ground truth metadata, did not faithfully simulate the difficulty of real user interactions.
Simulating realistic user behavior within automated benchmarks remains a challenge.
Distinguishing between these explanations will require evaluation with actual users in conversational settings.
The evaluation was fully autonomous with no human in the loop.
The evaluation did not include validation of the LLM judge against expert ratings.
A conversational interface where users can steer and correct would reveal patterns that single-turn evaluation cannot.

The cBio Cancer Genomics Portal is an open-access resource for interactive exploration of multidimensional cancer genomics data sets.
The portal currently provides access to data from more than 5,000 tumor samples from 20 cancer studies.
The cBio Cancer Genomics Portal significantly lowers the barriers between complex genomic data and cancer researchers.
The portal provides rapid, intuitive, and high-quality access to molecular profiles and clinical attributes from large-scale cancer genomics projects.
The portal empowers researchers to translate these rich data sets into biologic insights and clinical applications.
WebLogo generates sequence logos, graphical representations of the patterns within a multiple sequence alignment.
Sequence logos provide a richer and more precise description of sequence similarity than consensus sequences.
Sequence logos can rapidly reveal significant features of the alignment otherwise difficult to perceive.
Each logo consists of stacks of letters, one stack for each position in the sequence.
The overall height of each stack indicates the sequence conservation at that position, measured in bits.
The height of symbols within the stack reflects the relative frequency of the corresponding amino or nucleic acid at that position.
WebLogo has been enhanced recently with additional features and options.
WebLogo provides a convenient and highly configurable sequence logo generator.
A command line interface and the complete, open WebLogo source code are available for local installation and customization.
Visualization is an integral aspect of genomics data analysis.
Algorithmic-statistical analysis and interactive visualization are most effective when used iteratively.
Epiviz is a web-based genome browser.
The Epivizr Bioconductor package allows interactive, extensible, and reproducible visualization.
Epiviz and Epivizr operate within a state-of-the-art data-analysis platform.
DNAPlotter is an interactive Java application for generating circular and linear representations of genomes.
DNAPlotter makes use of the Artemis libraries to provide a user-friendly method of loading in sequence files (EMBL, GenBank, GFF) as well as data from relational databases.
DNAPlotter filters features of interest to display on separate user-definable tracks.
DNAPlotter can be used to produce publication quality images for papers or web pages.
DNAPlotter is freely available under a GPL licence.
DNAPlotter can be downloaded for MacOSX, UNIX, and Windows.
DNAPlotter is available at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute websites.
The download link for DNAPlotter is http://www.sanger.ac.uk/Software/Artemis/circular/.
The growing popularity and diversity of genomic data demand portable and versatile genome browsers.
We present an open source programming library called GIVE that facilitates the creation of personalized genome browsers without requiring a system administrator.

By inserting HTML tags, one can add to a personal webpage interactive visualization of multiple types of genomics data, including genome annotation, 'linear' quantitative data, and genome interaction data.
GIVE includes a graphical interface called HUG (HTML Universal Generator) that automatically generates HTML code for displaying user chosen data.
The HTML code generated by HUG can be copy-pasted into a user's personal website or saved and shared with collaborators.
GIVE is available at: https://www.givengine.org/.
The Comparative Epigenome Browser (CEpBrowser) was developed to allow the public to perform multi-species epigenomic analysis.
The web-based CEpBrowser integrates sequencing-based epigenomic datasets.
The web-based CEpBrowser manages sequencing-based epigenomic datasets.
The web-based CEpBrowser visualizes sequencing-based epigenomic datasets.
Five key features were developed to maximize the efficiency of interspecies epigenomic comparisons.
CEpBrowser is a web application.
CEpBrowser is implemented with PHP, MySQL, C, and Apache.
The URL for CEpBrowser is http://www.cepbrowser.org/.
IslandViewer is a widely used web-based resource for the prediction and analysis of genomic islands (GIs) in bacterial and archaeal genomes.
Genomic islands (GIs) are clusters of genes of probable horizontal origin.
GIs are of high interest since they disproportionately encode genes involved in medically and environmentally important adaptations, including antimicrobial resistance and virulence.
A major new release of IslandViewer is reported, since the last release in 2013.
IslandViewer 3 incorporates a completely new genome visualization tool, IslandPlot.
IslandPlot enables, for the first time, interactive genome analysis and gene search capabilities using synchronized circular, horizontal, and vertical genome views.
More curated virulence factors and antimicrobial resistance genes have been incorporated into IslandViewer 3.
Homologs of virulence factors and antimicrobial resistance genes have been identified in closely related genomes using strict filters.
Pathogen-associated genes have been re-calculated for all pre-computed complete genomes.
IslandViewer 3 can now handle incomplete genomes for user-uploaded analyses.
An improved queuing system on compute nodes has been implemented to handle user demand.
IslandViewer 3 represents a significant new version of this GI analysis software.
The new features of IslandViewer 3 may make it more broadly useful for general microbial genome analysis and visualization.
Dalliance is a new genome viewer.
Dalliance offers a high level of interactivity while running within a web browser.
All data is fetched using the established distributed annotation system (DAS) protocol.
The DAS protocol makes it easy to customize the browser and add extra data.
Dalliance runs entirely within your web browser.
Dalliance relies on existing DAS server infrastructure.
Browsers for several mammalian genomes are available at http://www.biodalliance.org/.
The use of DAS means you can add your own data to these browsers.
The source code (Javascript) is available under the BSD license.
The source code is straightforward to install on your own web server.
The source code can be embedded within other documents.
Hi-C experiments study how genomes fold in 3D.
Hi-C experiments generate contact maps containing features as small as 20 bp and as large as 200 Mb.
Juicebox is a tool for exploring Hi-C and other contact map data.
Juicebox allows users to zoom in and out of Hi-C maps interactively, similar to how Google Earth users zoom in and out of geographic maps.
Maps can be compared to one another, or to 1D tracks or 2D feature sets.
Significant progress has been made to map chromatin structure at unprecedented resolution and scales.
We are short of tools that enable the intuitive visualization and navigation along the three-dimensional (3D) structure of chromatins.
Available tools are generally script-based or present basic features that do not easily enable the integration of genomic data along with 3D chromatin structure.
Many scientists find themselves in the obligation to hack tools designed for other purposes, such as tools for protein structure study.

We present HiC-3DViewer, a new browser-based interactive tool designed to provide an intuitive environment for investigators to facilitate the 3D exploratory analysis of Hi-C data along with many useful annotation functionalities.
The most important feature of HiC-3DViewer is the 1D-to-2D-to-3D mapping, which highlights genomic regions of interest interactively.
This feature enables investigators to explore their data at different levels or angles.
Investigators can superpose different genomic signals, such as ChIP-Seq and SNP, on the top of the 3D structure.
As a proof of principle, we applied HiC-3DViewer to investigate the quality of Hi-C data.
We used HiC-3DViewer to show the spatial binding of GATA1 and GATA2 along the genome.
HiC-3DViewer enables the visualization of inter- and intra-chromatin interactions.
HiC-3DViewer gives users the flexibility to customize the look-and-feel of the 3D structure with a simple click.
HiC-3DViewer is implemented in Javascript and Python, and is freely available at: http://bioinfo.au.tsinghua.edu.cn/member/nadhir/HiC3DViewer/.
Supplementary information, including a user manual and demo data, is also available at the website.
A genome browser is software that allows users to visualize DNA, protein, or other sequence features within the context of a reference sequence, such as a chromosome or contig.
The Generic Genome Browser (GBrowse) is an open-source browser developed as part of the Generic Model Organism Database project (Stein et al., 2002).
GBrowse can be configured to display genomic sequence features for any organism.
GBrowse is the browser used for the model organisms Drosophila melanogaster (Grumbling and Strelets, 2006) and Caenorhabditis elegans (Schwarz et al., 2006), among others.
The software package can be downloaded from the Web and run on a Windows, Mac OS X, or Unix-type system.
Version 1.64, as described in the original protocol, was released in November 2005.
The software is under active development and new versions are released about every six months.
This update includes instructions on updating existing data sources with new files from NCBI.
Combo is a comparative genome browser that provides a dynamic view of whole genome alignments along with their associated annotations.
Combo provides two different visualization perspectives.
The perpendicular (dot plot) view provides a dot plot of genome alignments synchronized with a display of genome annotations along each axis.
The parallel view displays two genome annotations horizontally, synchronized through a panel displaying local alignments as trapezoids.
Users can zoom to any resolution, from whole chromosomes to individual bases.
Users can select, highlight and view detailed information from specific alignments and annotations.
Combo is organism agnostic and can import data from a variety of file formats.
Combo is integrated as part of the Argo Genome Browser which also provides single-genome browsing and editing capabilities.
Argo is written in Java, runs on multiple platforms and is freely available for download.
Genome browsers support fast navigation through vast datasets.
Genome browsers provide interactive visual analytics functions.
Interactive visual analytics functions help scientists achieve deeper insight into biological systems.
We developed Integrated Genome Browser (IGB).
Integrated Genome Browser (IGB) is a highly configurable, interactive, and fast open source desktop genome browser.
We describe multiple updates to IGB, including all-new capabilities to display and interact with data from high-throughput sequencing experiments.
Example visualizations and analyses of datasets from RNA-Seq, ChIP-Seq, and bisulfite sequencing experiments are described.
Understanding results from genome-scale experiments requires viewing the data in the context of reference genome annotations and other related datasets.
We enhanced IGB's ability to consume data from diverse sources, including Galaxy, Distributed Annotation, and IGB-specific Quickload servers.
The IGB codebase was transformed into a modular, extensible platform for developers to create and deploy all-new visualizations of genomic data.
IGB is open source.
IGB is freely available from http://bioviz.org/igb.
Scientists use DNA sequence differences between an individual's genome and a standard reference genome to study the genetic basis of disease.
Such differences are called sequence variants.
Determining the impact of sequence variants in the cell is difficult because it requires reasoning about both the type and location of the variant across several levels of biological context.
In this design study, we worked with four analysts to design a visualization tool supporting variant impact assessment for three different tasks.
We contribute data and task abstractions for the problem of variant impact assessment.
We contribute the carefully justified design and implementation of the Variant View tool.
Variant View features an information-dense visual encoding that provides maximal information at the overview level.
Variant View contrasts with the extensive navigation required by currently-prevalent genome browsers.
We provide initial evidence that the tool simplified and accelerated workflows for these three tasks through three case studies.
We reflect on the lessons learned in creating and refining data and task abstractions that allow for concise overviews of sprawling information spaces.
Concise overviews of sprawling information spaces can reduce or remove the need for the memory-intensive use of navigation.
Comparison of DNA sequences from different species is a fundamental method for identifying functional elements in genomes.
The VISTA family of tools was created to assist biologists in comparing DNA sequences from different species.
The first VISTA server was launched in the summer of 2000.
The first VISTA server was designed to align long genomic sequences and visualize these alignments with associated functional annotations.
The VISTA site currently includes multiple comparative genomics tools.
The VISTA site provides users with capabilities to browse pre-computed whole-genome alignments of large vertebrate genomes and other groups of organisms with VISTA Browser.
The VISTA site allows users to submit their own sequences of interest to several VISTA servers for various types of comparative analysis.
The VISTA site provides detailed comparative analysis results for a set of cardiovascular genes.
The capabilities of the VISTA site are illustrated by the analysis of a 180 kb interval on human chromosome 5 that encodes for the kinesin family member 3A (KIF3A) protein.
High-throughput sequencing (HTS) technologies provide an unprecedented capacity for data generation.
There is a corresponding need for efficient data exploration and analysis capabilities.
Most existing tools for HTS data analysis are developed for either automated purposes (e.g., genotyping) or visualization purposes (e.g., genome browsing).
Such tools are most powerful when combined.
Integration of visualization and computation allows users to iteratively refine their analyses by updating computational parameters within the visual framework in real-time.
The second version of the Savant Genome Browser is introduced as a standalone program for visual and computational analysis of HTS data.
Savant substantially improves upon its predecessor and existing tools by introducing innovative visualization modes and navigation interfaces for several genomic datatypes.
Savant synergizes visual and automated analyses in a way that is powerful yet easy even for non-expert users.
A number of plugins were developed by the Savant Community to demonstrate the power of integrating visual and automated analyses using Savant.
The Savant Genome Browser is freely available (open source) at www.savantbrowser.com.
UCSC Xena is a web-based visual integration and exploration tool for multi-omic data and associated clinical and phenotypic annotations.
Researchers can view and explore public data, their own private data, or both using the Xena Browser.
Private data are kept on the researcher's computer and are never uploaded to public servers.
UCSC Xena supports Mac, Windows, and Linux.
Xena showcases seminal cancer genomics datasets from TCGA, the Pan-Cancer Atlas, GDC, PCAWG, ICGC, and more.
Xena provides access to more than 1500 datasets across 50 cancer types.

Xena supports virtually any type of functional genomics data, including SNPs, INDELs, copy number variation, gene expression, ATAC-seq, DNA methylation, exon-, transcript-, miRNA-, lncRNA-expression, and structural variants.
Xena also supports clinical data such as phenotype information, subtype classifications, and biomarkers.
All data is available for download via Python or R APIs, or using URL links.
The Visual Spreadsheet view shows multiple data types side-by-side, enabling discovery of correlations across and within genes and genomic regions.

Xena provides dynamic Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, powerful filtering and subgrouping, differential gene expression analysis, charts, statistical analyses, genomic signatures, and the ability to generate URLs to live views.
Xena links out to the UCSC Genome Browser, MuPIT/CRAVAT, and TumorMap.
New features include genome-wide differential gene expression analysis.
New features include the ability to select samples directly from the screen for filtering and creating subgroups.
New features include violin plots on any numerical data.
New features include loading of Microsoft Excel files.
The beta prototype site for visualizing single-cell data delivers million-cell-scale multi-omics data for interactive visualization in a web browser.
Contact UCSC Xena for access to the beta prototype site for single-cell data visualization.

Hilbert curves enable high-resolution visualization of genomic data on a chromosome- or genome-wide scale.
The HilbertCurve package provides an easy-to-use interface for mapping genomic data to Hilbert curves.
The package transforms the curve as a virtual axis, hiding the details of the curve construction from the user.
HilbertCurve supports multiple-layer overlay, making it a powerful tool to correlate the spatial distribution of multiple feature types.
The HilbertCurve package and documentation are freely available from the Bioconductor project: http://www.bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/html/HilbertCurve.html

Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies have enabled the rapid generation of data on molecular aspects such as gene regulation, chromatin dynamics, and the three-dimensional organization of DNA.
The variation in biological context and the increasingly dispersed mode of data generation imply a need for precise, interoperable, and flexible representations of genomic features.
These representations should use formats that are easy to parse.
A host of alternative formats are currently available and in use, complicating analysis and tool development.
The issue of whether and how the multitude of formats reflects varying underlying characteristics of data has not previously been systematically treated.
Intrinsic distinctions between genomic features are identified.
The distinctions imply that a certain variation in the representation of features as genomic tracks is warranted.
Four core informational properties of tracks are discussed: gaps, lengths, values, and interconnections.
Fifteen generic track types are delineated based on the core informational properties.
Major existing representational formats are characterized based on track type distinctions.
The track types are not adequately supported by any single format.
In contrast to XML formats, none of the existing tabular formats are conveniently extendable to support all track types.
Two unified formats for track data are proposed: an improved XML format, BioXSD 1.1, and a new tabular format, GTrack 1.0.
The defined track types capture relevant distinctions between genomic annotation tracks.
The distinctions result in varying representational needs and analysis possibilities.
The proposed formats are GTrack 1.0 and BioXSD 1.1.
GTrack 1.0 and BioXSD 1.1 cater to the identified track distinctions.
GTrack 1.0 and BioXSD 1.1 emphasize preciseness, flexibility, and parsing convenience.
The Ensembl database project provides a bioinformatics framework to organise biology around the sequences of large genomes.
The Ensembl database is a comprehensive source of stable automatic annotation of the human genome sequence.
The database includes confirmed gene predictions integrated with external data sources.
The Ensembl database is available as either an interactive web site or as flat files.
The Ensembl project is an open source software engineering initiative to develop a portable system able to handle very large genomes.
The system addresses requirements from sequence analysis to data storage and visualisation.
The Ensembl site is one of the leading sources of human genome sequence annotation.
The Ensembl site provided much of the analysis for publication by the international human genome project of the draft genome.
The Ensembl system is being installed around the world in both companies and academic sites.
The system is being deployed on machines ranging from supercomputers to laptops.
Current synteny visualization tools focus on small regions of sequence and do not illustrate genome-wide trends.
Current synteny visualization tools are complicated to use and create visualizations that are difficult to interpret.
The Comparative Genomics Platform (CoGe) has developed two web-based tools to visualize synteny across whole genomes.
SynMap2 allows researchers to explore whole genome synteny patterns across two genomes in responsive, web-based visualization environments.
SynMap3D allows researchers to explore whole genome synteny patterns across three genomes in virtual reality environments.
Both tools have access to the extensive CoGe genome database containing over 30,000 genomes.
Users have the option to upload their own data to the tools.
By leveraging modern web technologies, there is no installation required for the tools.
The tools are widely accessible and easy to use.
Both tools are open source (MIT license) and freely available for use online through CoGe.
SynMap2 can be accessed at http://genomevolution.org/coge/SynMap.pl.
SynMap3D can be accessed at http://genomevolution.org/coge/SynMap3D.pl.
Source code is available at https://github.com/LyonsLab/coge.
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
High-throughput technologies rapidly generate genome-scale data.
It is important to visually integrate genome-scale data.
Visual integration of genome-scale data enables specific hypotheses to be formulated and tested.
MochiView is a platform-independent Java software.
MochiView integrates browsing of genomic sequences, features, and data.
MochiView provides DNA motif visualization and analysis.
MochiView is designed to be visually appealing and user-friendly.
The software is particularly useful for organizing, exploring, and analyzing large genomic datasets.
The datasets include those from deep RNA sequencing, chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments (ChIP-Seq and ChIP-Chip), and transcriptional profiling.
MochiView provides an extensive suite of utilities to identify connections between genomic datasets and short sequence motifs present in DNA or RNA.
MochiView provides an extensive suite of utilities to explore connections between genomic datasets and short sequence motifs present in DNA or RNA.
The number of completely sequenced genomes is continuously rising.
The increasing number of sequenced genomes allows for comparative analyses of genomic variation.
Comparative analyses of genomic variation are often based on whole-genome alignments.
Whole-genome alignments elucidate structural differences arising from insertions, deletions, or rearrangement events.
Computational tools are needed to visualize genome alignments in a meaningful manner.
Such visualizations help researchers gain new insights into the underlying data.
Genome visualizations are typically realized in a linear fashion as in genome browsers.
Genome visualizations can also use a circular approach where relationships between genomic regions are indicated by arcs.
Both linear and circular visualization methods allow for the integration of additional information such as experimental data or annotations.
Providing a visualization that allows for quick and comprehensive interpretation of all important genomic variations together with various supplemental data remains a challenge.
We propose the SuperGenome concept for the computation of a common coordinate system for all genomes in a multiple alignment.
The SuperGenome coordinate system allows for the consistent placement of genome annotations in the presence of insertions, deletions, and rearrangements.
We present the GenomeRing visualization that creates an interactive overview visualization of the multiple genome alignment in a circular layout.
The GenomeRing visualization is based on the SuperGenome.
We applied our methods to an alignment of Campylobacter jejuni strains for the discovery of genomic islands.
We applied our methods to an alignment of Helicobacter pylori, which we visualized in combination with gene expression data.
GenomeRing and example data is available at http://it.inf.uni-tuebingen.de/software/genomering/.
Fast algorithms are required for the comprehensive analysis of genomic and transcriptomic next-generation sequencing data.
Well-arranged visualizations are required for the comprehensive analysis of genomic and transcriptomic next-generation sequencing data.
The size of genomic and transcriptomic next-generation sequencing data is ever-growing.
ReadXplorer is a software offering straightforward visualization and extensive analysis functions for genomic and transcriptomic DNA sequences mapped on a reference.
A unique specialty of ReadXplorer is the quality classification of the read mappings.
The quality classification of the read mappings is incorporated in all analysis functions and displayed in ReadXplorer's various synchronized data viewers.
ReadXplorer's synchronized data viewers include (i) the reference sequence, (ii) its base coverage as a normalizable plot, (iii) histogram, (iv) read alignments, and (v) read pairs.

ReadXplorer's analysis capability covers RNA secondary structure prediction, single nucleotide polymorphism and deletion-insertion polymorphism detection, genomic feature and general coverage analysis.
For RNA-Seq data, ReadXplorer offers differential gene expression analysis, transcription start site and operon detection, as well as RPKM value and read count calculations.
ReadXplorer can combine or superimpose coverage of different datasets.
ReadXplorer is available as open-source software.
ReadXplorer is available at http://www.readxplorer.org along with a detailed manual.
HiGlass is an open source visualization tool built on web technologies.
HiGlass provides a rich interface for rapid, multiplex, and multiscale navigation of 2D genomic maps alongside 1D genomic tracks.
HiGlass allows users to combine various data types, synchronize multiple visualization modalities, and share fully customizable views with others.
HiGlass is useful for exploring different experimental conditions.
HiGlass is useful for comparing the results of analyses.
HiGlass is useful for creating interactive snapshots to share with collaborators and the broader public.
HiGlass is accessible online at http://higlass.io.
HiGlass is available as a containerized application that can be run on any platform.
Gepard provides a user-friendly, interactive application for the quick creation of dotplots.
Gepard utilizes suffix arrays to reduce the time complexity of dotplot calculation to Theta(m*log n).
Gepard includes a client-server mode, which is a novel feature for dotplot creation software.
The client-server mode allows the user to calculate dotplots and color them by functional annotation without any prior downloading of sequence or annotation data.
Source codes are available at http://mips.gsf.de/services/analysis/gepard.
Executable binaries are available at http://mips.gsf.de/services/analysis/gepard.
Sequence Bundles is a novel data visualization method for representing multiple sequence alignments (MSAs).
Sequence Bundles addresses key limitations of existing bioinformatics data visualization methods, such as the Sequence Logo.
Sequence Bundles enables salient visual expression of sequence motifs and other data features.
Sequence motifs and other data features would otherwise remain hidden using existing methods.
The development of Sequence Bundles employed research-led information design methodologies.
Sequences are encoded as uninterrupted, semi-opaque lines plotted on a 2-dimensional reconfigurable grid.
Each line represents a single sequence.
The thickness and opacity of the stack at each residue in each position indicates the level of conservation.
The lines' curved paths expose patterns in correlation and functionality.
Several MSAs can be visualised in a composite image.
The Sequence Bundles method is designed to favour a tangible, continuous and intuitive display of information.
A software demonstration application was developed for generating a Sequence Bundles visualisation of MSAs provided for the BioVis 2013 redesign contest.
The visualised line patterns were explored to discover interesting features in the dataset.
Reported features include the extreme conservation of sequences displaying a specific residue.
Reported features include bifurcations of the consensus sequence.
Sequence Bundles is a novel method for visualisation of MSAs and the discovery of sequence motifs.
Sequence Bundles can aid in generating new insight and hypothesis making.
Sequence Bundles is well disposed for future implementation as an interactive visual analytics software.
Sequence Bundles can complement existing visualisation tools.
Analysis of RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) data revealed that the vast majority of human genes express multiple mRNA isoforms.
These mRNA isoforms are produced by alternative pre-mRNA splicing and other mechanisms.
Most alternative isoforms vary in expression between human tissues.
As RNA-Seq datasets grow in size, it remains challenging to visualize isoform expression across multiple samples.
Sashimi plots are a quantitative visualization of aligned RNA-Seq reads.
Sashimi plots enable quantitative comparison of exon usage across samples or experimental conditions.
Sashimi plots can be made using the Broad Integrated Genome Viewer.
