Features in feature sets usually are of the same type, meaning they are either point or segment features and are associated with the same attributes.
Contiguous feature sets can encode the partitioning of a sequence into 'coding' and 'non-coding' regions.
Features with ordinal or quantitative attributes can be encoded by contiguous sets of features of different extents associated with an ordinal value.
Epigenomic data can be encoded by contiguous sets of non-overlapping features of equal size.
The reference sequence corresponds to a contiguous set of valued point features since each point is associated with a nucleotide.
Feature sets can be combined by intersecting them.
Feature sets can be combined by uniting them.
A set of sparse features, such as coding region, can be combined with a set of contiguous features encoding for an epigenetic signal across the sequence.
Features in the resulting set are associated with two attributes: the epigenetic signal and a Boolean attribute that encodes whether they are in a coding region.
Pairs of features can be connected via interconnection features.
In a map, an interconnection feature can be understood as a link between regions.
An example of an interconnection feature is a link showing the number of daily transatlantic flights between Europe and the US.
In a genomic sequence context, interconnection features can encode chromosome rearrangements.
If two segments of two chromosomes are swapped (translocation), it can be encoded with an interconnection feature which links the two subsequences.
Like other features, an interconnection feature can also be associated with attributes such as the type of the interconnection ('translocation') or a quantitative value.
Interconnection features can connect features within a sequence or between sequences.
Interconnection features can refer to no interconnections.
Feature sets are usually associated with meta data.
A feature set containing expression data of a patient sample can be associated with data about the sample itself and the sample donor.
The associated data can include the date when the sample was taken, the type of tissue, whether the donor has cancer, or whether the donor is a smoker.
In the map example, meta data could include the date when the map was created or the type of the map.
Meta data helps put the data into context.
Meta data can help identify possible correlations between different phenotypes and measured data.
A sequence can be visualized in any layout preserving the sequential nature.
Most genomic visualizations display sequential data either in a linear or a circular fashion.
The genomic coordinates of a sequence correspond to a sequence axis, which is visualized in a layout.
A sequence axis is a coordinate system for genomic features.
Linear layouts are intuitive since they are easy to read, usually from left to right.
Genomic sequences can be extremely long, requiring zooming and panning.
Circular layouts are used when the displayed sequence itself is circular.
Circular layouts are used to display a non-circular sequence in a space-saving way.
Circular layouts are used to show interactions between different parts of the sequence(s) using a chord diagram.
Space-filling curves, such as Hilbert curves, are more space-efficient than circular layouts.
Space-filling curves are often used to display a global overview of the genome while maintaining the spatial distribution of features.
Space-filling curves can only show one feature set.
It is hard to visually estimate the distances between two positions of the sequence in space-filling curves.
A sequence can be displayed in a spatial layout where the 3-dimensional structure is shown.
A spatial visualization requires three spatial axes, yet there is only one sequence axis.
Abstraction is a way of reducing the space of a sequence to concentrate on specific regions.
Abstraction involves replacing parts of the sequence or the entire sequence with abstraction elements, such as symbols, while maintaining the order of the elements.
For example, when only exons are of interest, introns can be abstracted to a gap, a symbol, or completely filtered out.
Non-adjacent parts of the sequence become next to each other in the visualization after abstraction.
No tool applying a complete abstraction was identified in the literature research, which could correspond to replacing both exons and introns with symbols.
Eukaryotic genomes often consist of multiple chromosomes, which are distinct sequences.
Eukaryotic genomes are often visualized as one contiguous sequence by placing chromosomes end-to-end.
Some visualizations, especially when comparing genomes, treat chromosomes as separate elements.
Different chromosomes are the most common reason to display a sequence in separate parts.
A sequence could also be partitioned based on other factors, such as equally sized subsequences to show the entire sequence in multiple rows.
Axes of the same layout can be arranged in different ways.
Figure 5d illustrates different arrangements of axes, derived from Meyer et al. [MMP09].
Axes in a linear and circular layout can be displayed in a parallel $( = \circledcirc )$ or serial $( -- \infty )$ arrangement.
A serial circular arrangement corresponds to two sequence axes in a 'half-circle' layout.
Axes in linear layout can be visualized in an orthogonal arrangement.
The different arrangements can be used to visualize interconnection features.
The different arrangements can be used to compare two different sequences in the context of comparative genomics.
For genomic data, it is important to put multiple different data types into context to draw conclusions.
When analyzing mutations in a genome, it is useful to visualize them together with gene annotations to estimate their functional impact.
A genomic visualization often contains multiple tracks to analyze multiple data types at the same time.
A track is a visual representation of genomic data with one or multiple parallel sequence axes showing one feature set.
Typically, tracks are oriented horizontally, but in some tools, they can also be oriented vertically.
The annotations and mutations in the stated example are two feature sets represented by two separate tracks.
For each type of feature sets, a separate track type can be defined as proposed by Gundersen et al. [GKA∗11].
According to the authors, seven different basic track types can be defined (excluding interconnections).
For sparse feature sets, they developed four track types.
A track for a sparse feature set with only features of length 1 with zero attributes is called a point track.
The positions of all substitution mutations could be displayed with a point track.
When the features in a point track are associated with an attribute, such as the substituted nucleotide, the track corresponds to a valued point track.
Segment tracks can encode for the position and extent of genes.
Valued segment tracks can additionally show an attribute, such as the gene expression or gene name.
For contiguous feature sets, the track types correspond to ungapped versions of the previously described types.
Contiguous feature sets containing features with a length produce a genome partition track.
If the features are associated with an attribute, the track corresponds to a step function.
A valued point track without gaps corresponds to a function.
Gundersen et al. propose eight extended track types which can encode interconnection features.
Seven of the extended track types correspond to previously described types.
Pairs of features are associated with interconnections which can be directed and/or have a weight.
This review allows the association of multiple attributes or complex attributes to track elements and interconnections.
A track should be able to encode the distribution of different nucleotides at point mutations.
The distribution of different nucleotides at point mutations corresponds to a valued point with a complex attribute.
All described feature set types can theoretically be encoded with these track types.
Hi-C data is usually visualized in arrangements using more than one sequence axis.
In Hi-C data, all pairs of contiguous segments of a specific size in the genome (bins) are associated with an interaction frequency.
Interaction frequency in Hi-C data represents an undirected weighted interconnection.
Hi-C data is usually easier to display using two axes.
Tracks showing features on a single axis are called one-axis tracks.
Tracks showing data on two axes are called two-axes tracks.
A matrix is a special form of a two-axis track showing data on two sequence axes arranged orthogonally.
Some common visual encodings of tracks and matrices can be seen in Figure 6.
One of the most commonly used encodings is color.
Valued point tracks showing variants can be encoded by coloring corresponding to the variant type.
Valued segments showing genes can be colored by functional category or gene expression using a continuous color scale.
A sparse set of segment features can contain segments that can overlap.
Read data is an example of a sparse segment feature.
Sequencing reads can be mapped to long sequences and usually overlap.
Sequencing reads do not always cover the entire genome.
Overlapping segment features can be stacked in a way that avoids visual overlaps.
The stacking method avoids introducing unnecessary white space.
Categorical attributes are often represented with symbols, such as the encoding of substitution mutations with the letter of the altered nucleotide or symbols for deletions and insertions.
Nucleotides are often encoded using both color and symbol.
Features with continuous attributes can be encoded using heights.
Segments can be displayed as blocks with varying heights depending on the attribute value.
The function track type is usually encoded by using a line chart which spans the entire sequence.
Matrices can be used to display interconnection features.
Figure 6c shows a continuous attribute of an interconnection feature encoded using a heatmap.
The colors encode the attribute value, i.e., the weight of the interconnection.
The matrix in Figure 6e only shows which features are interconnected.
Undirected interconnection features, such as Hi-C data, can be encoded on a one-axis track.
For sets of undirected interconnection features, a matrix representation is symmetrical.
The symmetrical matrix can be cut in half along the diagonal, rotated, and mapped to sequence coordinates forming a track.
The value of an interconnection can be retrieved by following imaginary lines originating at two features in 45-degree angles.
This type of track encoding can show interconnection without a continuous attribute, as seen in Figure 6d.
Multiple tracks are often displayed in one visualization to correlate multiple feature sets.
Tracks using the same sequence axis can be stacked or overlaid and aligned by sequence coordinates.
Figure 6e shows an arrangement of an orthogonal two-axes track aligned with multiple tracks in a linear layout.
Orthogonal arrangements contain two axes and can be arranged with multiple other tracks and matrices vertically and horizontally.
Figure 6f shows a parallel two-axes track where each axis is aligned with multiple one-axis tracks.
The two coordinate systems of the axes in the two-axes track do not have to be aligned but can show different regions of the sequence to display interconnection features.
Aligning multiple space-filling tracks is rather uncommon and limited.
Space-filling layouts use space most effectively, making it hard to arrange tracks in parallel.
A parallel arrangement complicates the identification of the same coordinate across tracks.
Overlaid track alignments are more common than parallel arrangements.
Transparent colors can be used to avoid hiding features in overlaid track alignments.
Combining feature sets is another possibility instead of overlaying two tracks.
Features on a single sequence can be visualized using one or multiple sequence axes.
In comparative genomics, multiple sequences or reference genomes are analyzed to study genome evolution.
Two or more sequences are compared to find blocks of high similarity on the sequence level (conservation).
The analysis includes determining if the location, order, proximity, and orientation of these blocks is similar in the compared genomes (synteny).
The goal of visual encoding of sequence comparisons is connecting sequence coordinate systems to show regions of high similarity of the sequences.
Similar regions can be visualized using different techniques and visual encodings.
The size of sequences to be compared can vary greatly from small regions, such as genes, to entire chromosomes or entire genomes.
There are three basic techniques for visualizing sequence comparisons usually applied for genomic visualization.
The three techniques are: (i) comparison by alignment, (ii) comparison by connecting conserved blocks, and (iii) comparison by using dot plots.
Alignment-based techniques are used especially for the visualization of many small sequences.
Shared nucleotides are algorithmically aligned as described in Section 2.4.
This alignment represents a construction of a shared coordinate system and sequence axis.
Each sequence corresponds to a valued segment or point track that is aligned to the coordinate system.
Different coordinates for each sequence can be kept separate to visualize comparisons in one or multiple two-axes tracks.
Interconnection features between segments in two sequences can encode the positions and extents of syntenic regions.
Syntenic regions can be encoded by connecting them with lines or bands or by applying the same color.
Meyer et al. [MMP09] describe which combination of encoding, layout, and arrangement is most effective depending on the length of the displayed sequence.
Bands and parallel linear or serial circular arrangements are recommended for shorter sequences (up to chromosomes) to avoid too many crossing lines.
Color encoding is recommended for whole genome comparisons in parallel arrangements.
Orthogonal arrangements of sequence axes can show the similarity between every position or bin of positions of one sequence to every position or bin of positions in the other sequence.
The two sequences are arranged in a 90 degree angle spanning a comparison matrix.
If nucleotides or bins match between positions of the two genomes, a dot is drawn in the corresponding cell.
Similar regions form diagonal lines of dots.
With this technique insertions, deletions and inversions can be identified.
Three parameters of a genomic visualization are defined to categorize tools and techniques.
The first parameter is the number of views that show data mapped to genomic coordinates.
The second parameter is the number of scales used to analyze the data at the same time.
The third parameter is the number of foci, i.e., non-adjacent genomic segments that can be viewed independently.
A view is restricted to a set of one or multiple aligned tracks.
A view contains at most one two-axis track.
A visualization can consist of one or multiple views displaying features mapped to genomic coordinates.
Views in a visualization can be linked or independent.
A genome can be very large and analyzing it on different scales, such as the whole genome or single genes, can be of great value.
A view of the entire world provides a useful overview, but we cannot analyze the street structure of New York.
Some genome visualizations only allow visualizing sequences on one scale at a time.
Other genome visualizations provide multiple views to visualize the data on different scales.
In our taxonomy, a multi-scale visualization visualizes the data on multiple scales at the same time in multiple different views.
Single-scale visualizations can provide a zooming interaction.
A focus can be understood as a sliding window across the genome.
Only the region in this window can be analyzed.
Multiple foci enable users to look at distinct segments of a genome in parallel.
Multiple foci allow users to compare features which are dispersed across the genome.
Foci can be defined in a flexible way.
Foci are visualized in separate views.
Sequence abstraction is usually done in a previous step.
In the case of filtering, non-adjacent sequences are 'glued' together.
Arrangements of two sequence axes corresponding to the same sequence are used to facilitate the visualization of interconnection features.
For arrangements of multiple axes, another dimension for scale and focus must be added.
Figure 7 shows an example of foci in an arrangement with two axes.
Two different foci are shown in the tracks aligned to the linear axes.
The matrix spanned by the orthogonal arrangement can only visualize one focus of two-dimensional data.
Two orthogonal axes can be on different scales, leading to two one-axis scales and one two-axes scale.
Combining these parameters in all possible ways results in five basic view configurations of genomic visualizations.
If a visualization contains two axes, foci and scale refer to two-axes foci and two-axes scales.

Restricting a view to a set of one or multiple aligned tracks, with at most one two-axis track, makes it impossible to visualize multiple scales and foci of the highest dimension in one view with the proposed taxonomy.
The left branch of the taxonomy consists of only one path.
Other view configurations are combinations of multiple views with one or more scales and foci.
The tools are categorized in Sections 5 and 6 using five basic view configurations.
For visualizations with multiple axes, the number of one-axis foci and one-axis scales is additionally shown.
Genomic visualizations often incorporate multiple views.
Multiple views in genomic visualizations can be independent, weakly linked, medium linked, or strongly linked.
Independent views are not connected in any way.
Weakly linked views are connected by brushing and linking.
Medium linked views share navigation, such as when two views are at different scales but zooming affects both.
Strongly linked views share genomic coordinates on one axis and can also share tracks aligned to the axis.
Utility views provide information about tracks, features, or genomic coordinates.
Utility views never show genomic coordinates directly but only meta data or derived data.
Utility views can be either aligned with the genomic visualization or weakly linked.
An aligned utility visualization shows meta data about tracks situated on the left side of each track.
In sequencing or expression data, aligned utility visualizations can show phenotypic information about the sample donor.
Aligned utility visualizations are in direct association with genomic data and are called strongly connected utility visualizations.
A weakly connected utility visualization is connected with a table through brushing and linking.
In weakly connected utility visualizations, clicking on an element in the visualization highlights the corresponding element in the table and vice versa.
Weakly connected utility visualizations are not aligned with genomic data.
Visualization tasks represent actions that users may perform on their data.
Visualization tasks can be both low-level operations or high-level user intents while interacting with a system.
Visualization tasks have been defined and classified, often depending on the context and scope of the tasks.
A common feature of most genomic coordinate visualizations is that they visualize one or multiple types of features at their corresponding positions.
The tasks that different tools and techniques help to solve are often similar.
This section describes the most common tasks performed using genomic visualizations.
A typology of abstract visualization tasks was proposed by Brehmer and Munzner [BM13].
The typology focuses on three questions: why is a task performed, what are the inputs and outputs, and how is the task performed.
The typology distinguishes between user intents (that answer why) and interactions (that answer how).
The typology provides a link between the questions of why and how.
This section summarizes and categorizes the 'Why' task for genomic visualizations.
This section provides an overview of common interactions ('How') and inputs and outputs ('What').
The task topology described by Brehmer et al. [BM13] is adapted to genomic visualizations.
The adaptation starts with slight adjustments to the described search tasks LOOKUP, LOCATE, BROWSE, and EXPLORE.
In the task taxonomy, LOOKUP refers to viewing features at one position, such as navigating to a known gene and a specific feature set like gene expression.
LOCATE refers to finding one or multiple features with desired properties, such as locating peaks of an epigenetic signal or highly expressed genes in a single feature set.
BROWSE is similar to LOOKUP, but while the position is known, the feature set is unknown.
For example, different feature sets, such as expression and mutations, can be browsed at the position of a known gene.
EXPLORE refers to a very broad task where neither the position nor the feature set is known.
In EXPLORE, multiple feature sets at different positions in multiple loci are explored.
Exploring corresponds to a combination of other tasks, such as browsing features at positions or locating features in a feature set.
In exploration, the characteristics being looked for or the positions being browsed are not predefined and can change during the process.

The described tasks and the query tasks IDEN-TIFY, COMPARE, and SUMMARIZE proposed by Brehmer et al. [BM13] are categorized into single feature set, multi feature set, single locus, and multi locus tasks.
Table 1 provides the categorization of these tasks.
The task taxonomy illustration in Figure 1 shows how these tasks operate on genomic visualizations.
LOOKUP and IDENTIFY correspond to single feature set, single locus tasks.
LOOKUP aims to find the desired feature set at a locus.
IDENTIFY characterizes the feature attributes.
LOOKUP and IDENTIFY tasks are often paired, for example, after looking up an epigenetic signal at the position of a gene, we can identify the actual value of the signal.
LOCATE and COMPARE are single feature set, multi locus tasks.
LOCATE refers to finding positions.
COMPARE finds a relationship between features at the located positions.
For example, the expression levels of two genes can be compared.
The expression feature set of each gene has to be looked up before it can be compared.
The expression value has to be identified before it can be compared.
If feature sets are of the same type, COMPARE can also be applied across feature sets at the same locus.
EXPLORE is a search task.
The goal of SUMMARIZE is to find data patterns and trends.
Summarizing provides an overview or a 'big picture' of the data, such as 'expression levels of genes in this pathway are high'.
Summarizing can be done for a single feature set or a single locus.
After exploring the data or browsing a specific locus and identifying the feature attributes, the patterns in a single locus can be summarized.
For example, summarizing that a highly expressed gene has mutations in its promoter region.
Summarizing a single feature set can involve locating features with interesting attributes in a feature set while exploring the data.
By summarizing attributes of features in one set, the distribution of attributes can be characterized.
Tools for the visualization of genomic data often differ in their level of interactivity.
Many tools can only plot data as a static image.
Different datasets, visual representations, regions, and zoom levels can often be chosen as parameters for the plot.
There is no interaction with the visualization itself in many tools.
Interactive tools often offer navigation interactions to navigate along the sequence axis via zooming, panning, or jumping to regions.
Navigation is essential for most genomic tools due to the immense size of genomes, especially for the search tasks LOOKUP and LOCATE.
SELECTION interactions are often implemented for highlighting features or selecting them in order to derive a new visualization or feature.
Some tools allow rearranging views and tracks.
Some tools allow changing the visual encodings of features.
Flexible interactions enable a more in-depth exploration of the data and provide the users with details on demand.
A sequence can be abstracted.
Many tools offer sequence abstraction as an interaction.
Sequence abstraction is most commonly achieved by filtering introns or abstracting them using gaps.
It is often possible to filter out other regions that are not of interest.
Abstraction, especially by filtering introns, helps users explore the parts of the sequence that are the most informative for their problems.
AGGREGATION is often implemented together with zooming.
Features are encoded differently depending on the amount of space that is available.
A multiple sequence alignment can be displayed by showing every nucleotide individually when zoomed in.
A multiple sequence alignment can be displayed as blocks showing conserved parts when zoomed out.
By applying aggregation while zooming, the visualization remains informative on different scales.
Features can be EXPLORE-d and SUMMARIZE-d on multiple levels.
The input and output of a task depend heavily on the tool itself.
The input can consist of one or multiple feature sets depending on the type of the task.
The tasks LOOKUP, IDENTIFY, LOCATE, and COMPARE have a single feature set as input.
The task BROWSE works with multiple feature sets as input.
The tasks SUMMARIZE and EXPLORE can have one or multiple feature sets as input.
For single feature set tasks, the outputs are a combination of feature positions or feature attributes.
The output of the search task LOOKUP is a feature at a position.
The output of the search task BROWSE is a feature at a position.
The output of the search task LOCATE is one or multiple positions of features of interest.
The output of the search task IDENTIFY is the attributes of a feature.
The output of the search task COMPARE is a relationship between two or more attributes.
The outputs of EXPLORE and SUMMARIZE are not as easily defined.
Exploring can return everything starting from one feature at a position to multiple positions.
Exploring can return patterns of different types of features or correlations.
SUMMARIZE returns a statement about the data, such as the distribution of the attributes in a set of features.
SUMMARIZE returns the relation between multiple sets of features.
Differentiating between low-level and high-level tasks is important for characterizing genomic visualization tools.
Low-level tasks help model how a tool works.
High-level tasks correspond more to biological questions.
The tasks described are low-level tasks.
Most of the tools in Sections 5 and 6 support low-level tasks for exploring the data.
Tools differ in the biological questions that users want to solve with a tool.

Biological questions can range from broad questions, such as 'How does sequencing data from a cancer sample compare to the reference genome?' to specific questions, such as 'Is TP53 mutated in this sample?'
The biological question determines the low-level tasks.
To answer broad questions, users must explore the data by browsing positions of interest and locating peaks in tracks.
While exploring, users summarize their insights.
Users summarize insights by navigating along coordinates, arranging tracks, changing encodings, filtering introns, and performing other interactions depending on the tool.
Biological questions depend heavily on the input data and user intent.
Genome-scale visualizations display one or multiple regions of a genome on absolute coordinates.
Genome-scale visualizations are categorized based on the type of features they specialize in.
Genome-scale visualizations can focus on displaying noninterconnected feature sets.
Genome-scale visualizations can focus on displaying sparsely interconnected feature sets.
Genome-scale visualizations can focus on displaying densely interconnected feature sets.
Non-interconnected feature sets are often visualized using tools with one or multiple parallel tracks.
These tools visualize many kinds of different features.
Features are displayed using linear, circular, and space-filling layouts.
Certain data types are very common in visualization tools.
Some tools are specialized for visualizing specific types of genomic data, such as the Savant Genome.
The table includes genes TP53, MDM2, MDM4, and CDKN2A.
The table appears to organize relationships or data involving TP53, MDM2, MDM4, and CDKN2A.
Browser 2 [FSB<sup>∗</sup>12] is specialized in showing structural variation.
HilbertVis [And09] and HilbertCurve [GES16] are especially useful to display epigenetic data.
Tools in this section are specialized in visualizing many sets of non-interconnected features.
These tools can sometimes visualize local interconnections.
Genome browsers usually display multiple parallel tracks in a linear layout.
A genome browser commonly consists of three components: a reference genome, annotations, and one or multiple tracks.
Figure 9 from the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) [TRM13] illustrates this structure.
Genome browsers are used for exploring a reference genome together with other knowledge-based data.
Genome browsers are used for comparing experimental results, such as sequencing data, to the reference genome.
Genome browsers usually enable the visualization of a small window of the genome and allow navigation such as zooming and panning.
Most genome browsers are not suited for meaningful overview visualizations of whole genomes, since the data must be extremely aggregated to fit on the screen.
Most genome browsers are limited to the visualization of single chromosomes.
Some genome browsers apply a predefined minimum zoom level.
Other genome browsers show empty tracks for certain feature sets if the visualization is zoomed out too much.
Genome browsers often consist of a single view and can therefore only visualize the data at one scale and focus at a time (1-1-1 view configuration).
Features can only be explored, compared, and summarized in a relatively small window, which complicates analyzing gene co-expression in non-adjacent regions.
Some tools provide methods of data abstraction, with which introns can be filtered out or specific regions of interest can be placed next to each other.
In these tools, the regions are still visualized in the same view, and to change the borders of the regions they have to be redefined.
The Savant Genome Browser [FSB<sup>∗</sup>12] is the only feature viewer grouped into the multiple views, single scale, and single focus (n-1-1 view configuration).
The Savant Genome Browser consists of two visualizations both showing features on genomic coordinates.
One visualization is a classic genome browser view.
The additional view can display population data with different visualizations.
The additional view can display a heatmap showing the patterns of alterations of single bases in multiple samples.
In the heatmap, columns correspond to the positions of the alterations, rows correspond to samples, and cells show the type of alteration.
Although the heatmap shows the data on a different scale, it is associated with a single scale configuration.
The heatmap does not display the same data (the same tracks) on a different scale but constitutes an entirely different visualization.
Overview-detail genome browsers are another category of genome browsers.
Overview-detail genome browsers use an n-n-1 view configuration.
Overview-detail genome browsers show one region of the genome, which means they have one focus.
Overview-detail genome browsers also have an additional detailed view for a part of the chosen region.
Navigation in overview-detail genome browsers is usually linked to ensure that the detailed view is always part of the chosen region.
An advantage of the overview-detail genome browser layout is that features can be analyzed in a small window as well as in their global neighborhood simultaneously.
Few genome browsers provide a very high level of flexibility by enabling the visualization of multiple focus regions on different scales.
The n-n-n view configuration allows the visualization of multiple focus regions on different scales.
Initially, genome browsers visualize single regions, but multiple regions can be selected or added through different mechanisms.
IGV allows selecting a region with a user dialog.
The NCBI Sequence Viewer enables the creation of new views by highlighting a region and selecting 'create new panel' in a context menu.
Regions can be selected with different extents, yet they receive the same amount of screen space.
The two region views can show features on different scales.
Region views can be arranged horizontally in IGV.
Region views can be arranged vertically in the NCBI Sequence Viewer.
A horizontal arrangement facilitates comparing tracks, but the available horizontal space for each region is smaller.
The increased flexibility of genome browsers in an n-n-n view configuration often goes along with a more complicated user interface and more possible interactions.
For problems that do not require viewing different scales and regions at the same time, a genome browser in a less flexible configuration can facilitate the exploration process.
Genome browsers often contain utility views strongly connected to the tracks.
Utility views in genome browsers show different kinds of metadata.
Different tracks in genome browsers correspond to data obtained by analyzing different samples.
For example, IGV [TRM13] can display data about the sample donor.
Sample donor data can include gender, race, ethnicity, and more.
Xena is a type of visualization for noninterconnected feature sets.
Xena can be seen as a 'population browser.'
Unlike a genome browser, Xena enables the exploration of entire patient cohorts.
Xena displays population data in a column-based layout, where each column corresponds to a view showing a different type of feature.
Sample data is displayed as parallel tracks in each column.
Tracks are sorted by columns, while the order is preserved across columns.
Columns can either show meta data about the samples or genomic data, such as gene expression, copy number alterations, or somatic mutations for small regions such as genes.
Columns can be added, sorted, and rearranged interactively.
In contrast to genome browsers, the focus of Xena is not on visualizing data on genomic coordinates, but on stratifying and characterizing populations.
What is considered meta data and utility views in our taxonomy can be seen as main data types and main views in Xena.
Circular layouts are often used for the visualization of non-interconnected feature sets.
These visualizations are commonly known as 'genome maps'.
Circular genome maps provide an overview of the entire genome and allow summarizing genomic features on a global scale.
Circular genome maps usually visualize prokaryotic genomes, which are circular and much smaller than eukaryotic genomes.
Figure 10 shows an example of a genome map created with CiVi.
Despite smaller genomes, data still has to be aggregated to be visualized.
Even the smallest known prokaryotic genome is larger than 500 kilo bases.
Contiguous feature sets with quantitative attributes are averaged for windows of equal size, and only segments bigger than a minimum size are displayed.
Many tools provide the possibility to visualize the entire genome in a linear layout.
Some tools allow visualizing a small region of the genome in a linear layout.
Most genome maps are static plotting tools and do not provide direct interactivity.
Some genome maps allow zooming and navigating the genome map.
Island Viewer 3 is an example of a more interactive prokaryotic genome visualization.
Island Viewer 3 can visualize one or two prokaryotic genomes in parallel in an overview-detail configuration (n-n-1).
Island Viewer 3 uses a circular layout for the genome overview and a linear layout for the details.
Island Viewer 3 is specialized compared to other described circular visualizations.
Island Viewer 3 focuses on a specific data type called genomic islands.
Island Viewer 3 compares different prediction methods for genomic islands.
Space-Filling Layout is a visualization technique for chromosome or genome-wide overviews of features, especially epigenomic marks.
The technique is based on a genome layout that uses a space-filling curve rather than a linear or circular genome layout.

A desirable property of space-filling curves, such as the Hilbert curve, is that they arrange 1D sequence information on a 2D grid so that features close to each other in 1D are close to each other in 2D.
Such plots can be created with HilbertVis and the HilbertCurve R package.
Unlike linear and circular genome layouts, parallel arrangements of tracks are not feasible for space-filling curve layouts.
The space-filling curve approach is limited to single or a limited number of overlaid tracks.
Sparsely interconnected feature sets correspond to a set of segment features with interconnections that are sparsely distributed across the genome.
Researchers often deal with sparsely interconnected feature sets when studying structural variation or alternative splicing.
Structural variation and alternative splicing are based on mapping reads to the genome and deducting patterns from this mapping.
Patterns of alternative splicing can be found by mapping reads obtained with RNA sequencing to a DNA sequence.
Splicing patterns can be deducted based on the number of reads per exon and reads that contain sequences of multiple exons (junction reads).
Genomic rearrangements are obtained by mapping DNA sequencing reads to the genome.
Rearrangements can be found by analyzing read depth, paired-end reads, and reads containing sequences of distant regions (split reads).
Sparsely interconnected feature sets are commonly visualized in a linear or circular layout.
The main goals for visualizing sparsely interconnected feature sets are exploring the data and comparing patterns across different samples and conditions.
For genomic rearrangement, both the global distribution of the arrangements and patterns on the sequence level are of interest for exploration.
Alternative splicing is usually visualized in a linear layout.
Alternative splicing is sometimes displayed as a track in a genome browser.

MGcV facilitates tasks such as the interactive annotation of gene function, the discovery of regulatory elements, or the sequence-based reconstruction of gene regulatory networks.

MGcV can be used in gene function annotation by visually integrating information on prokaryotic genes, like their annotation as available from NCBI with other annotation data such as Pfam domains, sub-cellular location predictions, and gene-sequence characteristics such as GC content.

MGcV provides interactive features that allow the graphical selection of genes to facilitate data gathering, such as upstream regions, IDs, or annotation, in the analysis and reconstruction of transcription regulation.
Putative regulatory elements and their corresponding scores or data from RNA-seq and microarray experiments can be uploaded, visualized, and interpreted in ranked comparative context maps.
Ranked maps allow the interpretation of predicted regulatory elements and experimental data in light of each other.
MGcV advances the manual comparative analysis of genes and regulatory elements.
MGcV provides fast and flexible integration of gene-related data.
MGcV enables straightforward data retrieval.
MGcV is available at http://mgcv.cmbi.ru.nl.
CiVi is a user-friendly web-based tool to create custom circular maps for analyzing microbial genomes and sequence elements.
Sequence-related data such as gene-name, COG class, PFAM domain, GC%, and subcellular location can be comprehensively viewed using CiVi.
Quantitative gene-related data, such as expression ratios or read counts, can be uploaded and visualized in CiVi.
Predicted sequence elements, such as regulatory sequences, can also be uploaded and visualized in CiVi.
CiVi allows visual interpretation of genomic elements in the context of their genome-wide distribution.
CiVi allows visual interpretation of genomic elements in the context of provided experimental data.
CiVi allows visual interpretation of genomic elements in the context of their local orientation and location with respect to neighboring genes.
CiVi enables both experts and non-experts to integrate public genome data with genome analysis results in circular genome maps suitable for publication.
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
CiVi is freely available at http://civi.cmbi.ru.nl.
GView is a Java application for viewing and examining prokaryotic genomes in a circular or linear context.
GView accepts standard sequence file formats to generate genome maps.
GView allows the use of an optional style specification file to generate customizable, publication quality genome maps.
GView generates genome maps in bitmap and scalable vector graphics formats.
GView features an interactive pan-and-zoom interface.
GView provides a command-line interface for incorporation in genome analysis pipelines.
GView includes a public Application Programming Interface for incorporation in other Java applications.
GView is a freely available application licensed under the GNU Public License.
The application, source code, documentation, file specifications, tutorials, and image galleries are available at http://gview.ca.
SpliceSeq is a resource for RNA-Seq data that provides a clear view of alternative splicing.
SpliceSeq identifies potential functional changes that result from splice variation.
SpliceSeq displays intuitive visualizations of splicing events.
SpliceSeq provides prioritized lists of results that highlight splicing events and their biological consequences.
SpliceSeq unambiguously aligns reads to gene splice graphs.
SpliceSeq facilitates accurate analysis of large, complex transcript variants that cannot be adequately represented in other formats.
SpliceSeq is freely available at http://bioinformatics.mdanderson.org/main/SpliceSeq:Overview.
The application is a Java program that can be launched via a browser.
The application can also be installed locally.
Local installation requires MySQL.
Local installation requires Bowtie.
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
We present an update to our Galaxy-based web server for processing and visualizing deeply sequenced data.

The core tool set, deepTools, allows users to perform complete bioinformatic workflows ranging from quality controls and normalizations of aligned reads to integrative analyses, including clustering and visualization approaches.
Since we first described our deepTools Galaxy server in 2014, we have implemented new solutions for many requests from the community and our users.
We introduce significant enhancements and new tools to further improve data visualization and interpretation.
deepTools continue to be open to all users and freely available as a web service at deeptools.ie-freiburg.mpg.de.
The new deepTools2 suite can be easily deployed within any Galaxy framework via the toolshed repository.
We provide source code for command line usage under Linux and Mac OS X.
A public and documented API for access to deepTools functionality is also available.
Contact mapping experiments such as Hi-C explore how genomes fold in 3D.
Juicebox.js is a cloud-based web application for exploring Hi-C datasets.
Juicebox.js allows users to zoom in and out of Hi-C datasets using an interface similar to Google Earth.
Juicebox.js has features designed to facilitate data reproducibility and sharing.
Juicebox.js encodes the exact state of the browser in a shareable URL.
Creating a public browser for a new Hi-C dataset does not require coding and can be accomplished in under a minute.
The web app makes it possible to create interactive figures online that can complement or replace ordinary journal figures.
When combined with Juicer, Juicebox.js makes the entire process of data analysis transparent.
Every step from raw reads to published figure is publicly available as open source code when using Juicebox.js and Juicer.
We propose a method for predicting splice graphs that enhances curated gene models using evidence from RNA-Seq and EST alignments.

Results obtained using RNA-Seq experiments in Arabidopsis thaliana show that predictions made by our SpliceGrapher method are more consistent with current gene models than predictions made by TAU and Cufflinks.
Analysis of plant and human data indicates that the machine learning approach used by SpliceGrapher is useful for discriminating between real and spurious splice sites.
The machine learning approach used by SpliceGrapher can improve the reliability of detection of alternative splicing.
SpliceGrapher is available for download at http://SpliceGrapher.sf.net.
Alternative splicing is a process by which the same DNA sequence is used to assemble different proteins, called protein isoforms.
Alternative splicing works by selectively omitting some of the coding regions (exons) typically associated with a gene.
Detection of alternative splicing is difficult and uses a combination of advanced data acquisition methods and statistical inference.
Knowledge about the abundance of isoforms is important for understanding both normal processes and diseases.
Knowledge about the abundance of isoforms is important to eventually improve treatment through targeted therapies.
The data is complex and current visualizations for isoforms are neither perceptually efficient nor scalable.
We developed Vials, a novel visual analysis tool that enables analysts to explore the various datasets that scientists use to make judgments about isoforms.
The datasets include the abundance of reads associated with the coding regions of the gene, evidence for junctions (edges connecting the coding regions), and predictions of isoform frequencies.
Vials is scalable as it allows for the simultaneous analysis of many samples in multiple groups.
Vials enables experts to identify patterns of isoform abundance in groups of samples.
Vials enables experts to evaluate the quality of the data.
We demonstrate the value of our tool in case studies using publicly available datasets.
Identifying syntenic regions, i.e., blocks of genes or other markers with evolutionary conserved order, is a central goal in comparative genomics.
Quantifying evolutionary relatedness between genomes in terms of chromosomal rearrangements is a central goal in comparative genomics.
The analysis of synteny and the resulting assessment of genome rearrangements are sensitive to the choice of a number of arbitrary parameters.
The detection of synteny blocks is affected by the choice of a set of markers.
The detection of synteny blocks is affected by different aggregation strategies that enable coarse graining of synteny blocks and exclusion of micro-rearrangements.
Existing tools and resources that facilitate identification, visualization, and analysis of synteny need to be further improved.
Improved tools should provide a flexible platform for synteny analysis, especially in the context of multiple genomes.
Cinteny is a new tool for fast identification and analysis of synteny with different sets of markers and various levels of coarse graining of syntenic blocks.
Cinteny uses the Hannenhalli-Pevzner approach and its extensions.
Cinteny enables interactive determination of evolutionary relationships between genomes in terms of the number of rearrangements (the reversal distance).
Cinteny integrates synteny browsing with assessment of evolutionary distances for multiple genomes.
Cinteny provides flexibility to adjust the parameters and re-compute the results on-the-fly.
Cinteny can work with user-provided data, such as orthologous genes, sequence tags, or other conserved markers.
Cinteny provides many annotated mammalian, invertebrate, and fungal genomes that are pre-loaded and available for analysis.
Cinteny is available for analysis at http://cinteny.cchmc.org.
Cinteny allows automatic comparison of multiple genomes.
Cinteny performs sensitivity analysis for synteny block detection.
Cinteny performs sensitivity analysis for the subsequent computation of reversal distances.
Cinteny can be used to interactively browse syntenic blocks conserved in multiple genomes.
Cinteny facilitates genome annotation and validation of assemblies for newly sequenced genomes.
Cinteny can be used to construct and assess phylogenomic trees.
A graphical method is presented for displaying the patterns in a set of aligned sequences.
The characters representing the sequence are stacked on top of each other for each position in the aligned sequences.
The height of each letter is made proportional to its frequency.
The letters are sorted so the most common one is on top.
The height of the entire stack is adjusted to signify the information content of the sequences at that position.
From these 'sequence logos', one can determine the consensus sequence.
From these 'sequence logos', one can determine the relative frequency of bases at every position in a site or sequence.
From these 'sequence logos', one can determine the information content (measured in bits) at every position in a site or sequence.
The logo displays both significant residues and subtle sequence patterns.
Sequence Logos and its variants are the most commonly used method for visualization of multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and sequence motifs.
Sequence Logos provide consensus-based summaries of the sequences in the alignment.
Individual sequences cannot be identified in the visualization using Sequence Logos.
Covariant sites are not easily discernible in Sequence Logos visualizations.
Sequence Bundles is a motif visualization technique that maintains a one-to-one relationship between sequences and their graphical representation.
Sequence Bundles visualizes covariant sites.
Alvis is an open-source platform for the joint explorative analysis of MSAs and phylogenetic trees.
Alvis employs Sequence Bundles as its main visualization method.
Alvis combines the power of the visualization method with an interactive toolkit allowing detection of covariant sites, annotation of trees with synapomorphies and homoplasies, and motif detection.
Alvis offers numerical analysis functionality, such as dimension reduction and classification.
Alvis is user-friendly, highly customizable and can export results in publication-quality figures.
Alvis is available as a full-featured standalone version (http://www.bitbucket.org/rfs/alvis).
The Sequence Bundles visualization module is further available as a web application (http://science-practice.com/projects/sequence-bundles).
CGView (Circular Genome Viewer) is a Java application and library for generating high-quality, zoomable maps of circular genomes.
CGView converts XML or tab-delimited input into a graphical map in PNG, JPG, or Scalable Vector Graphics format.
The graphical map includes sequence features, labels, legends, and footnotes.
The program can generate a series of hyperlinked maps showing expanded views in addition to the default full view map.
The linked maps can be explored using any Web browser.
The linked maps allow rapid genome browsing and facilitate data sharing.
CGView is available as a standalone application, library, or applet.
Sample input, sample maps, and documentation for CGView can be obtained from http://wishart.biology.ualberta.ca/cgview/.
Data visualization is an essential component of genomic data analysis.
The size and diversity of data sets produced by sequencing and array-based profiling methods present major challenges to visualization tools.
The Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) is a high-performance viewer that efficiently handles large heterogeneous data sets.
IGV provides a smooth and intuitive user experience at all levels of genome resolution.
A key characteristic of IGV is its focus on the integrative nature of genomic studies.
IGV supports both array-based and next-generation sequencing data, and the integration of clinical and phenotypic data.
IGV is often used to view genomic data from public sources.
The primary emphasis of IGV is to support researchers who wish to visualize and explore their own data sets or those from colleagues.
IGV supports flexible loading of local and remote data sets.
IGV is optimized to provide high-performance data visualization and exploration on standard desktop systems.
IGV is freely available for download from http://www.broadinstitute.org/igv, under a GNU LGPL open-source license.
Two Sample Logo is a web-based tool that detects and displays statistically significant differences in position-specific symbol compositions between two sets of multiple sequence alignments.
In a typical scenario, two groups of aligned sequences will share a common motif but will differ in their functional annotation.
The inclusion of the background alignment provides an appropriate underlying amino acid or nucleotide distribution.
The inclusion of the background alignment addresses intersite symbol correlations.
The difference detection process is sensitive to the sizes of the aligned groups.
Two Sample Logo extends WebLogo, a widely-used sequence logo generator.
The source code is distributed under the MIT Open Source license agreement.
The source code is available for download free of charge.
Galaxy HiCExplorer is a web server that facilitates the study of the 3D conformation of chromatin by allowing Hi-C data processing, analysis, and visualization.
Galaxy HiCExplorer enables users with little bioinformatic background to perform every step of Hi-C data analysis in one workflow.

The workflow includes mapping of the raw sequence data, creation of Hi-C contact matrices, quality assessment, correction of contact matrices, and identification of topological associated domains (TADs) and A/B compartments.
Users can create publication-ready plots of the contact matrix, A/B compartments, and TADs on a selected genomic locus.
Additional information like gene tracks or ChIP-seq signals can be included in the plots.
Galaxy HiCExplorer is freely usable at: https://hicexplorer.usegalaxy.eu.
Galaxy HiCExplorer is available as a Docker container: https://github.com/deeptools/docker-galaxy-hicexplorer.
Large, complex genomic datasets are increasingly easy to generate.
The number of publicly available datasets in cancer and other diseases is rapidly growing.
The lack of intuitive, easy-to-use analysis tools has remained a barrier to the effective use of such data.
WebMeV is an open-source, web-based tool that gives users access to sophisticated tools for analysis of RNA-Seq and other data.
WebMeV is designed to democratize data access.
WebMeV combines cloud-based technologies with a simple user interface.
WebMeV allows users to access large public datasets, such as that from The Cancer Genome Atlas, or to upload their own datasets.
The interface allows users to visualize data and to apply advanced data mining analysis methods.
Users can explore the data and draw biologically meaningful conclusions using WebMeV.
We provide an overview of WebMeV and demonstrate two simple use cases.
The use cases illustrate the value of putting data analysis in the hands of those exploring the underlying biology of studied systems.
RNA sequencing has provided unprecedented resolution of alternative splicing.
RNA sequencing has provided unprecedented resolution of splicing quantitative trait loci (sQTL).
There are few tools available for visualizing the genotype-dependent effects of splicing at a population level.
SplicePlot is a simple command line utility that produces intuitive visualization of sQTLs and their effects.
SplicePlot takes mapped RNA sequencing reads in BAM format as input.
SplicePlot takes genotype data in VCF format as input.
SplicePlot outputs publication-quality Sashimi plots, hive plots, and structure plots.
SplicePlot enables better investigation and understanding of the role of genetics on alternative splicing and transcript structure.
Source code and detailed documentation are available at http://montgomerylab.stanford.edu/spliceplot/index.html under Resources and at Github.
SplicePlot is implemented in Python.
SplicePlot is supported on Linux and Mac OS.
A VirtualBox virtual machine running Ubuntu with SplicePlot already installed is also available.
Jalview Version 2 is a system for interactive WYSIWYG editing, analysis, and annotation of multiple sequence alignments.
Core features of Jalview Version 2 include keyboard and mouse-based editing.
Core features of Jalview Version 2 include multiple views and alignment overviews.
Core features of Jalview Version 2 include linked structure display with Jmol.
Jalview 2 is available as a lightweight Java applet for use in web applications.

Jalview 2 is available as a powerful desktop application that employs web services for sequence alignment, secondary structure prediction, and the retrieval of alignments, sequences, annotation, and structures from public databases.
Jalview 2 supports retrieval of data from any DAS 1.53 compliant sequence or annotation server.
The Jalview 2 Desktop application is made freely available under the GPL.
The JalviewLite applet is made freely available under the GPL.
The applications can be downloaded from www.jalview.org.
The 3D Genome Browser allows users to explore their own chromatin interaction data and over 300 publicly available datasets.
The 3D Genome Browser supports chromatin interaction data of different types.
A new binary data format for Hi-C data reduces file size by at least a magnitude.
The new binary data format allows users to visualize chromatin interactions over millions of base pairs within seconds.
The browser provides multiple methods to link distal cis-regulatory elements with their potential target genes.
Users can integrate thousands of other omics data to gain a comprehensive view of the regulatory landscape and 3D genome structure.
We introduce ggbio, a new methodology to visualize and explore genomics annotations and high-throughput data.
The plots provide detailed views of genomic regions.
The plots provide summary views of sequence alignments and splicing patterns.
The plots provide genome-wide overviews with karyogram, circular, and grand linear layouts.
The methods leverage the statistical functionality available in R.
The methods leverage the grammar of graphics.
The methods leverage the data handling capabilities of the Bioconductor project.
The plots are specified within a modular framework that enables users to construct plots in a systematic way.
The plots are generated directly from Bioconductor data structures.
The ggbio R package is available at http://www.bioconductor.org/packages/2.11/bioc/html/ggbio.html.
The MSAViewer is a JavaScript component for visualization and analysis of Multiple Sequence Alignment data of any size.
Core features of the MSAViewer include interactive navigation through the alignment.
Core features of the MSAViewer include application of popular color schemes.
Core features of the MSAViewer include sorting, selecting, and filtering.
The MSAViewer is written entirely in JavaScript and is compatible with modern web browsers.
The MSAViewer does not require any specialized software.
The MSAViewer is part of the BioJS collection of components.
The MSAViewer is released as open source software under the Boost Software License 1.0.
Documentation, source code, and the viewer are available at http://msa.biojs.net.
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
